papers.title: Tracking the Best Linear Predictor
papers.abstract: In most on-line learning research the total on-line loss of the algorithm is compared to the total loss of the best off-line predictor u from a comparison class of predictors. We call such bounds static bounds. The interesting feature of these bounds is that they hold for an arbitrary sequence of examples. Recently some work has been done where the predictor ut at each trial t is allowed to change with time, and the total on-line loss of the algorithm is compared to the sum of the losses of ut at each trial plus the total "cost" for shifting to successive predictors. This is to model situations in which the examples change over time, and different predictors from the comparison class are best for different segments of the sequence of examples. We call such bounds shifting bounds. They hold for arbitrary sequences of examples and arbitrary sequences of predictors. Naturally shifting bounds are much harder to prove. The only known bounds are for the case when the comparison class consists of a sequences of experts or boolean disjunctions. In this paper we develop the methodology for lifting known static bounds to the shifting case. In particular we obtain bounds when the comparison class consists of linear neurons (linear combinations of experts). Our essential technique is to project the hypothesis of the static algorithm at the end of each trial into a suitably chosen convex region. This keeps the hypothesis of the algorithm well-behaved and the static bounds can be converted to shifting bounds.

findings.summary: Predictions can exceed the range assumed by the proof. Allowed data sequences violate the advertised error guarantee, so it does not hold for the stated class of sparse predictors.

papers.title: Regularized Principal Manifolds
papers.abstract: Many settings of unsupervised learning can be viewed as quantization problems - the minimization of the expected quantization error subject to some restrictions. This allows the use of tools such as regularization from the theory of (supervised) risk minimization for unsupervised learning. This setting turns out to be closely related to principal curves, the generative topographic map, and robust coding. We explore this connection in two ways: (1) we propose an algorithm for finding principal manifolds that can be regularized in a variety of ways; and (2) we derive uniform convergence bounds and hence bounds on the learning rates of the algorithm. In particular, we give bounds on the covering numbers which allows us to obtain nearly optimal learning rates for certain types of regularization operators. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of the approach.

findings.summary: A continuous kernel has eigenfunctions that lack the uniform bound used in the analysis. This contradicts the claimed covering estimate and undermines the learning rates supported by it.
findings.claim: A Mercer kernel with eigenvalues lambda_n=O(exp(−alpha n^p)) induces a quadratic-regularizer ball with log N(epsilon,F,L_infinity)=O(log^((p+1)/p)(1/epsilon)); this supplies the entropy hypothesis for the nearly optimal spectral learning rates in Corollary7.

findings.explanation: Mercer continuity does not imply a common finite supremum bound on all normalized eigenfunctions. An explicit continuous kernel with a complete L2 eigenbasis and exact sorted spectrum exp(−n²) has a compact unit RKHS ball whose log uniform covering number is at least of order epsilon^−2 along a sequence, contradicting the asserted log^(3/2)(1/epsilon) entropy bound.

findings.impact: The covering-number reduction and resulting nearly optimal spectral learning-rate claims are an explicit central theoretical contribution in the abstract and Section7. Proposition5 is false under its stated assumptions; its use in deriving Corollary7 leaves that advertised general spectral guarantee unsupported. Existing compactness and bounded-output restrictions hold in the counterexample. Repair requires a substantive additional localization/eigenfunction assumption and revised scope plus verification of the rate claims, not a changed constant or local equation correction. The algorithm and Gaussian feasibility examples may remain useful, but the affected theoretical contribution requires major revision. This does not claim that every actual quantization-risk rate is false solely because this covering proof fails.

papers.title: Classes of Kernels for Machine Learning: A Statistics Perspective
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present classes of kernels for machine learning from a statistics perspective. Indeed, kernels are positive definite functions and thus also covariances. After discussing key properties of kernels, as well as a new formula to construct kernels, we present several important classes of kernels: anisotropic stationary kernels, isotropic stationary kernels, compactly supported kernels, locally stationary kernels, nonstationary kernels, and separable nonstationary kernels. Compactly supported kernels and separable nonstationary kernels are of prime interest because they provide a computational reduction for kernel-based methods. We describe the spectral representation of the various classes of kernels and conclude with a discussion on the characterization of nonlinear maps that reduce nonstationary kernels to either stationarity or local stationarity.

findings.summary: The proposed general kernel formula excludes some valid kernels while admitting invalid ones. Its claimed characterization and associated recipe for constructing nonstationary kernels therefore fail as stated.
findings.claim: The asserted necessary-and-sufficient spectral characterization of the most general nonstationary kernel class, and the proposal to design arbitrary nonstationary kernels by choosing the measure in (19).
findings.location: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 308), Section 4, Equation (19) and the paragraph introducing it; related spectral claim begins PDF p. 9 (printed p. 307), last displayed equation.
findings.explanation: The cosine representation forces simultaneous inversion symmetry, excluding smooth bounded rank-one PSD kernels. Moreover, a nonnegative finite symmetric spectral measure need not produce even a nonnegative diagonal.
findings.evidence: For every F, the right side of (19) obeys K(-x,-z)=K(x,z). But K(x,z)=exp(-(x-1)^2-(z-1)^2)=g(x)g(z), g(x)=exp(-(x-1)^2), is a bounded C-infinity kernel by (6), and K(1,1)=1 whereas K(-1,-1)=exp(-8). Thus necessity fails independently of any interpretation of positive measure. Under the ordinary nonnegative interpretation explicitly written in the paper, F=(delta_(0,1)+delta_(1,0)+delta_(0,-1)+delta_(-1,0))/4 is finite and symmetric under coordinate exchange and simultaneous reversal; (19) gives K=(cos(x)+cos(z))/2 and Gram at {0,pi} is diag(1,-1). A further exact necessity check is sin(x)sin(z): K00=0 would force the total mass of any nonnegative F to vanish although K(pi/2,pi/2)=1.
findings.impact: Spectral representation and spectral design of the various kernel classes are an explicit main contribution in the abstract, introduction and conclusion; (19) is presented as the complete characterization for the most general class. It excludes ordinary smooth bounded kernels already valid under the paper's own construction (6), while its stated measure assumptions can manufacture negative variances. Fixing it requires changing the spectral representation (including complex/sine contributions where needed), adding the essential spectral PSD constraint, and delimiting the class for which the representation exists. Consequently the central general nonstationary design result is invalid as written; this is not a harmless normalization or an isolated example typo.

papers.title: Graph-Based Hierarchical Conceptual Clustering
papers.abstract: Hierarchical conceptual clustering has proven to be a useful, although under-explored, data mining technique. A graph-based representation of structural information combined with a substructure discovery technique has been shown to be successful in knowledge discovery. The SUBDUE substructure discovery system provides one such combination of approaches. This work presents SUBDUE and the development of its clustering functionalities. Several examples are used to illustrate the validity of the approach both in structured and unstructured domains, as well as to compare SUBDUE to the Cobweb clustering algorithm. We also develop a new metric for comparing structurally-defined clusterings. Results show that SUBDUE successfully discovers hierarchical clusterings in both structured and unstructured data.

findings.summary: The quality score can improve simply because a clustering covers less data, with everything else unchanged. This conflicts with its proposed role as an objective measure of clustering quality.
findings.claim: The new hierarchical clustering quality measure rewards greatest coverage with fewest clusters while accounting for description size and overlap, and supplies objective quantitative validation/comparison.

Repair requires redesigning the evaluation measure and re-evaluating comparisons, not a local proof correction preserving current results. The separate clustering mechanism may remain useful; its validity does not establish the failed general metric or claimed objective superiority.

papers.title: Stability and Generalization
papers.abstract: We define notions of stability for learning algorithms and show how to use these notions to derive generalization error bounds based on the empirical error and the leave-one-out error. The methods we use can be applied in the regression framework as well as in the classification one when the classifier is obtained by thresholding a real-valued function. We study the stability properties of large classes of learning algorithms such as regularization based algorithms. In particular we focus on Hilbert space regularization and Kullback-Leibler regularization. We demonstrate how to apply the results to SVM for regression and classification.

findings.summary: The proof treats stability on training examples as stability on unseen examples. A learner meeting the assumptions violates the resulting certificate, so it can understate prediction error.

papers.title: Machine Learning with Data Dependent Hypothesis Classes
papers.abstract: We extend the VC theory of statistical learning to data dependent spaces of classifiers. This theory can be viewed as a decomposition of classifier design into two components; the first component is a restriction to a data dependent hypothesis class and the second is empirical risk minimization within that class. We define a measure of complexity for data dependent hypothesis classes and provide data dependent versions of bounds on error deviance and estimation error. We also provide a structural risk minimization procedure over data dependent hierarchies and prove consistency. We use this theory to provide a framework for studying the trade-offs between performance and computational complexity in classifier design. As a consequence we obtain a new family of classifiers with dimension independent performance bounds and efficient learning procedures.

findings.summary: The classifier count overlooks the choice of training subsample. The complexity bound can certify a learner that memorizes training data yet performs poorly on unseen examples.
findings.claim: Predetermining sample indices for sphere centers and their radii gives data-dependent shatter coefficient 1 and the associated dimension-independent performance guarantees.

One advertised trivial-computation variant would receive a sharply false error certificate despite almost maximal risk. Repair requires accounting for an exponentially large subsample class at q=n, materially changing the claimed complexity tradeoff rather than correcting a constant or typo. The generic theorem with the true coefficient and the separate variable-center consistency result are not claimed false.

papers.title: Rademacher and Gaussian Complexities: Risk Bounds and Structural Results
papers.abstract: We investigate the use of certain data-dependent estimates of the complexity of a function class, called Rademacher and Gaussian complexities. In a decision theoretic setting, we prove general risk bounds in terms of these complexities. We consider function classes that can be expressed as combinations of functions from basis classes and show how the Rademacher and Gaussian complexities of such a function class can be bounded in terms of the complexity of the basis classes. We give examples of the application of these techniques in finding data-dependent risk bounds for decision trees, neural networks and support vector machines.

findings.summary: The proof omits permitted negative coefficient choices. The resulting bound assigns zero complexity to a class that fits arbitrary labels, undermining its use as a learning guarantee.
findings.claim: The data-dependent Gaussian complexity bound for l1-constrained two-layer neural networks and its use in margin risk/model-selection bounds.

The erroneous geometry measure erases the complexity of arbitrarily rich classifiers and gives a false risk certificate with probability1. Adding signed coordinates preserves a generic dimension rate but restores an essential missing common-mode term; this changes the claimed geometry guarantee by an unbounded amount. Generic risk and other structural theorems are not asserted false.

papers.title: Algorithmic Luckiness
papers.abstract: Classical statistical learning theory studies the generalisation performance of machine learning algorithms rather indirectly. One of the main detours is that algorithms are studied in terms of the hypothesis class that they draw their hypotheses from. In this paper, motivated by the luckiness framework of Shawe-Taylor et al. (1998), we study learning algorithms more directly and in a way that allows us to exploit the serendipity of the training sample. The main difference to previous approaches lies in the complexity measure; rather than covering all hypotheses in a given hypothesis space it is only necessary to cover the functions which could have been learned using the fixed learning algorithm. We show how the resulting framework relates to the VC, luckiness and compression frameworks. Finally, we present an application of this framework to the maximum margin algorithm for linear classifiers which results in a bound that exploits the margin, the sparsity of the resultant weight vector, and the degree of clustering of the training data in feature space.

findings.summary: The sparse replacement preserves training labels without preserving losses on unseen examples. The main margin-based estimate can be exponentially too small and does not provide its claimed control.
findings.claim: The maximum-margin luckiness based on training margin, expansion sparsity and training-data clustering is omega-small with omega=(2em/(-L0))^(-2L0), independent of delta.

Every selected easy training half in a family has unique maximum-margin output and luckiness exactly-8, yet the same lucky set realizes all2^128 probe loss patterns. A constant/typo correction cannot recover the claimed polynomial complexity at fixed luckiness; the training-only approximation does not establish the required full-sample cover.

papers.title: The Set Covering Machine
papers.abstract: We extend the classical algorithms of Valiant and Haussler for learning compact conjunctions and disjunctions of Boolean attributes to allow features that are constructed from the data and to allow a trade-off between accuracy and complexity. The result is a general-purpose learning machine, suitable for practical learning tasks, that we call the set covering machine. We present a version of the set covering machine that uses data-dependent balls for its set of features and compare its performance with the support vector machine. By extending a technique pioneered by Littlestone and Warmuth, we bound its generalization error as a function of the amount of data compression it achieves during training. In experiments with real-world learning tasks, the bound is shown to be extremely tight and to provide an effective guide for model selection.

findings.summary: The argument counts probability twice after conditioning. This substantially understates the classifier's error certificate, affecting both the reported guarantee and model selection based on it.

papers.title: Finding the Most Interesting Patterns in a Database Quickly by Using Sequential Sampling
papers.abstract: Many discovery problems, e.g. subgroup or association rule discovery, can naturally be cast as n-best hypotheses problems where the goal is to find the n hypotheses from a given hypothesis space that score best according to a certain utility function. We present a sampling algorithm that solves this problem by issuing a small number of database queries while guaranteeing precise bounds on the confidence and quality of solutions. Known sampling approaches have treated single hypothesis selection problems, assuming that the utility is the average (over the examples) of some function --- which is not the case for many frequently used utility functions. We show that our algorithm works for all utilities that can be estimated with bounded error. We provide these error bounds and resulting worst-case sample bounds for some of the most frequently used utilities, and prove that there is no sampling algorithm for a popular class of utility functions that cannot be estimated with bounded error. The algorithm is sequential in the sense that it starts to return (or discard) hypotheses that already seem to be particularly good (or bad) after a few examples. Thus, the algorithm is almost always faster than its worst-case bounds.

The full loop accepts only g at m1, c at m2, d at m3 and excludes a, giving gap.27>.1 with probability1. General n+1 family has gap .9 n epsilon. The proof verifies I3 only for the newly accepted hypothesis, although decreasing n strengthens I3 for prior outputs.
findings.impact: This refutes the algorithm’s central generic guarantee, even conditional on every confidence interval being correct. Error inflation grows with n, so no fixed missing constant repairs the statement. A corrected method must change approximation budgeting/acceptance or add substantive estimator restrictions with a new proof; the reported behavior of that revised algorithm is not established.

papers.title: MISEP – Linear and Nonlinear ICA Based on Mutual Information
papers.abstract: Linear Independent Components Analysis (ICA) has become an important signal processing and data analysis technique, the typical application being blind source separation in a wide range of signals, such as biomedical, acoustical and astrophysical ones. Nonlinear ICA is less developed, but has the potential to become at least as powerful. This paper presents MISEP, an ICA technique for linear and nonlinear mixtures, which is based on the minimization of the mutual information of the estimated components. MISEP is a generalization of the popular INFOMAX technique, which is extended in two ways: (1) to deal with nonlinear mixtures, and (2) to be able to adapt to the actual statistical distributions of the sources, by dynamically estimating the nonlinearities to be used at the outputs. The resulting MISEP method optimizes a network with a specialized architecture, with a single objective function: the output entropy. The paper also briefly discusses the issue of nonlinear source separation. Examples of linear and nonlinear source separation performed by MISEP are presented.

findings.summary: The entropy formula omits multiple input branches when the neural transformation folds space. The objective can prefer dependent outputs, contradicting its intended use for recovering independent components.
findings.claim: Maximizing the permitted nonlinear network's log-Jacobian objective maximizes its actual output entropy and supplies the central mutual-information-based nonlinear ICA criterion, while separately learning marginal CPFs.
findings.location: Section 2.3.2, original PDF page 6 (printed 1302), equation H(z)=H(o)+<log|det J|> and ensuing empirical training objective E; affected nonlinear-MI interpretation in Section 2.2, PDF page 5, and conclusions PDF page 19. Network constraints on PDF page 6; general F and direct links on PDF pages 5, 7–9 and 11–12.
findings.explanation: The change-of-variables identity omits conditional preimage-branch entropy when the learned joint separating MLP F is noninjective. Scalar auxiliary monotonicity and sampled nonsingular Jacobians do not enforce global injectivity. The omitted term varies with network parameters and can cause the objective to prefer dependent folded components.
findings.evidence: Latent X,V iid Uniform[−1,1], observations o1=X+V/100,o2=V (dependent, det mixing1,H(o)=ln4). Let phi=2atan/pi, g(x)=phi(x+1)−phi(x−1), mid=(g(0)+g(1))/2; separator F1=15(g(X)−mid)−3, F2=V+X/10−2, where X=o1−o2/100. F1 uses three arctan hidden units, F2 direct links. Each psi_i is an eight-unit increasing arctan mixture with output weights1/8 (norm1/sqrt8), hidden input8, positive biases at negative quantile thresholds. All z lie in [−1,1]^2. Certified E_fold=[.1760211810,.1922129252]>0 implies claimed H(z)>ln4, above the maximum bounded-output entropy. True MI=(1−ln2)/20=.01534264097>0. Conditional branch entropy=.95ln2. An independent inverse-linear comparator has E=[−.3326859502,−.3218725029], MI0 and greater actual entropy; objective ordering is reversed with gap>.49789. Ideal CPFs still give E_fold=ln2−.05>0 vs independent0. Source-forward port on 4096 dependent observations gives minabsdet .0660422678,2048 determinants each sign, and empirical E .19061147, passing actual1e−10 sampled cutoff. Restoring validity requires global injectivity constraints or accounting for preimages, changing the allowed nonlinear model/optimization, rather than repairing a constant or local formula. Linear ICA and the historical illustrative empirical runs are not claimed false.

papers.title: Statistical Dynamics of On-line Independent Component Analysis
papers.abstract: The learning dynamics of on-line independent component analysis is analysed in the limit of large data dimension. We study a simple Hebbian learning algorithm that can be used to separate out a small number of non-Gaussian components from a high-dimensional data set. The de-mixing matrix parameters are confined to a Stiefel manifold of tall, orthogonal matrices and we introduce a natural gradient variant of the algorithm which is appropriate to learning on this manifold. For large input dimension the parameter trajectory of both algorithms passes through a sequence of unstable fixed points, each described by a diffusion process in a polynomial potential. Choosing the learning rate too large increases the escape time from each of these fixed points, effectively trapping the learning in a sub-optimal state. In order to avoid these trapping states a very low learning rate must be chosen during the learning transient, resulting in learning time-scales of O(N2) or O(N3) iterations where N is the data dimension. Escape from each sub-optimal state results in a sequence of symmetry breaking events as the algorithm learns each source in turn. This is in marked contrast to the learning dynamics displayed by related on-line learning algorithms for multilayer neural networks and principal component analysis. Although the natural gradient variant of the algorithm has nice asymptotic convergence properties, it has an equivalent transient dynamics to the standard Hebbian algorithm.

findings.summary: A nonlinear transformation of Gaussian data introduces a nonzero mean and covariance between projections that the analysis omits. The advertised description of learning several components therefore does not follow from the stated dynamics.
findings.claim: The new multiprojection even-nonlinearity dynamics is a scalar-noise diffusion in the displayed cubic potential, yielding the K-dependent barrier f(K) and parallel-extraction inference.
findings.location: PDF page 10 (printed 1402), Equation (17); repeated page 13 Equation (22), page 16 Equation (25); scalar diffusion/potential-barrier application on pages 8 and 11 (Figure 4, left).
findings.explanation: For phi(y)=y², the Gaussian nonlinearity has nonzero mean, creating a leading cross-projection covariance omitted by the diagonal tensor. Correct whitening produces a non-gradient drift, so a scalar-D/polynomial-barrier repair is unavailable.
findings.evidence: Take A=I_N,W=(e3,e4), K=M=2, sources +2 with p=1/5 and -1/2 otherwise. At R=0,Q=I, sigma=I and eta=nu N^-3/2, scaled noise covariance for (r11,r21) is exactly [[3,1],[1,3]], versus Eq17 diag(3,3). Off-diagonal nu²N^-2 is leading at every N. With C=[[3,1],[1,3]], correct drift F=-nu² C r/2+kappa3 nu r² and B=nu²C have curl(B^-1F)=kappa3(a-b)/(4nu), ruling out an isotropic scalar-potential description even after correcting the local cross-potential factor. Sample covariance [[2.99790,.99830],[.99830,2.99115]] agrees.
findings.impact: The paper identifies its analytical solution of multiprojection dynamics as a principal new contribution beyond prior single-source work. The even-nonlinearity branch uses an incorrect leading stochastic generator, and its scalar-noise escape/barrier solution must be replaced by a multidimensional quasipotential analysis, not a corrected scalar constant. The N²/N³ orders, qualitative trapping and transient equivalence are not refuted.

papers.title: On the Rate of Convergence of Regularized Boosting Classifiers
papers.abstract: A regularized boosting method is introduced, for which regularization is obtained through a penalization function. It is shown through oracle inequalities that this method is model adaptive. The rate of convergence of the probability of misclassification is investigated. It is shown that for quite a large class of distributions, the probability of error converges to the Bayes risk at a rate faster than n-(V+2)/(4(V+1)) where V is the VC dimension of the "base" class whose elements are combined by boosting methods to obtain an aggregated classifier. The dimension-independent nature of the rates may partially explain the good behavior of these methods in practical problems. Under Tsybakov's noise condition the rate of convergence is even faster. We investigate the conditions necessary to obtain such rates for different base classes. The special case of boosting using decision stumps is studied in detail. We characterize the class of classifiers realizable by aggregating decision stumps. It is shown that some versions of boosting work especially well in high-dimensional logistic additive models. It appears that adding a limited labelling noise to the training data may in certain cases improve the convergence, as has been also suggested by other authors.

findings.summary: A monotone classification region cannot be represented by a sum of decision stumps. This counterexample defeats the claimed complete characterization of which regions the model can represent.
findings.claim: The promised characterization of classifiers realizable by decision-stump ensembles: non-XOR / coordinate-permutable monotone sets are exactly additive threshold sets, with arbitrary L¹ approximation in the continuous zero-boundary-measure case.
findings.location: PDF pages 17–18 (printed 877–878), Definition 13, Theorem 14 and its (iii)⇒(i) proof, Theorem 15; boundary refinements on page 19 and Appendix C page 31 inherit the failed approximation claim.
findings.explanation: Monotone sets need not be additive thresholds. A four-variable monotone AND/OR set satisfies every defined non-XOR condition yet has an exact four-point obstruction; its continuous analogue has optimal stump-ensemble error exactly 1/16.
findings.evidence: On the full grid {0,1}^4, A=(x1 AND x2) OR (x3 AND x4) is monotone and has no one-coordinate XOR. Positive vertices 1100,0011 and negative vertices 1010,0101 obey f1100+f0011=f1010+f0101 for every additive f, contradicting correct signs. Under uniform [0,1]^4 with each bit indicating x_i>=1/2, A has boundary measure zero. Coupling the same low/high coordinate draws across the four corresponding orthants forces at least one error on every draw, so total L¹ error>=1/16 for any additive classifier. Weights (2,2,1,1), threshold7/2 attain exactly1/16.
findings.impact: The abstract/introduction identify the complete decision-stump realizability characterization as a principal contribution. Both its finite equivalence and continuous arbitrary-approximation theorem are false on a full four-dimensional cube; the approximation theorem predicts zero limiting error where the exact optimum is 1/16. A substantially stronger representability condition or different characterization is required. The separate oracle inequality and additive-risk rate claims are not refuted by this finding.

papers.title: On Inclusion-Driven Learning of Bayesian Networks
papers.abstract: Two or more Bayesian network structures are Markov equivalent when the corresponding acyclic digraphs encode the same set of conditional independencies. Therefore, the search space of Bayesian network structures may be organized in equivalence classes, where each of them represents a different set of conditional independencies. The collection of sets of conditional independencies obeys a partial order, the so-called "inclusion order." This paper discusses in depth the role that the inclusion order plays in learning the structure of Bayesian networks. In particular, this role involves the way a learning algorithm traverses the search space. We introduce a condition for traversal operators, the inclusion boundary condition, which, when it is satisfied, guarantees that the search strategy can avoid local maxima. This is proved under the assumptions that the data is sampled from a probability distribution which is faithful to an acyclic digraph, and the length of the sample is unbounded. The previous discussion leads to the design of a new traversal operator and two new learning algorithms in the context of heuristic search and the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method. We carry out a set of experiments with synthetic and real-world data that show empirically the benefit of striving for the inclusion order when learning Bayesian networks from data.

findings.summary: Unconditional reversals of certain graph edges change the posterior sampling distribution. The proposed sampler does not preserve its intended target, undermining its interpretation as posterior sampling.
findings.claim: The proposed eMC3 algorithm has the stated posterior as its stationary distribution and the added RCAR operation improves convergence to that posterior.
findings.location: PDF page 19 / printed 545, Figure 5; PDF page 24 / printed 550, Figure 7 lines 6–10; PDF page 23 / printed 549, Equation (6) and posterior-convergence claims; Section 5.3 PDF pages 32–43.
findings.explanation: Uniform covered-edge reversals are not posterior-invariant because covered-reversal degrees vary within a Markov equivalence class. Performing them unconditionally before an otherwise correct NR/NCR Hastings step changes the sampler target.
findings.evidence: For one fully observed binary record 000, every BDeu likelihood is 1/8. Under the score and uniform prior of Equation (6), interpreted on the actual DAG state space, the charitable target is uniform 1/25. Intended RCAR r=2 followed by correctly Hastings-adjusted NR changes complete-class mass from 6/25 to 37/150 in one step, and has stationary empty mass 247/6229 and complete-class mass 1536/6229. DAG TV is 2052/155725; class TV is 1239/155725. The chain is irreducible and aperiodic. Correcting ordinary Hastings alone therefore does not repair this issue.
findings.impact: The new MCMC algorithm is a central advertised contribution but fails its defining posterior-invariance requirement even with the correct ordinary Hastings step. Its claimed faster posterior convergence and posterior-weighted interpretation lack a valid common target. Repair requires a changed RCAR kernel and reassessment of the MCMC evidence, rather than a reporting correction; no historical Alarm ranking reversal is asserted.

findings.summary: The experiments omit a correction for unequal numbers of neighboring graphs. This invalidates the stated sampling implementation and prevents the convergence evidence from establishing the intended behavior.
findings.claim: The experimental MC3/eMC3 transition rules sample the stated posterior and their convergence comparisons and BMA quantities have a posterior interpretation.
findings.location: PDF page 32 / printed 558, Section 5.3.1 first paragraph; Equation (6) on PDF page 23 / printed 549; experimental Figures 10–17 and Section 5.3 Bayesian model averaging.

Empty NR degree2 versus edge degree1; omitted-ratio sampler has stationary thirds for every RCAR count. RCAR itself is target-invariant here. To avoid the coincidental uniform-class match in this two-variable example, rows 000/111 yield empty targets 1/79 under uniform DAG prior and 1/29 under uniform class prior, versus stationary 33/1579 for intended RCAR r2, 1/47 without RCAR, and 139/6449 after correcting RCAR alone. These chains are irreducible and aperiodic; stationary class distributions disagree with both target interpretations.
findings.impact: This invalidates the expressly described experimental MCMC implementation and therefore the central posterior-convergence/BMA evidence. Restoring the formula changes actual transition probabilities and calls for rerunning the comparisons; the graph-theory and heuristic HCMC contribution survives, but that does not establish the failed MCMC contribution.

papers.title: Learning Probabilistic Models: An Expected Utility Maximization Approach
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of learning a probabilistic model from the viewpoint of an expected utility maximizing decision maker/investor who would use the model to make decisions (bets), which result in well defined payoffs. In our new approach, we seek good out-of-sample model performance by considering a one-parameter family of Pareto optimal models, which we define in terms of consistency with the training data and consistency with a prior (benchmark) model. We measure the former by means of the large-sample distribution of a vector of sample-averaged features, and the latter by means of a generalized relative entropy. We express each Pareto optimal model as the solution of a strictly convex optimization problem and its strictly concave (and tractable) dual. Each dual problem is a regularized maximization of expected utility over a well-defined family of functions. Each Pareto optimal model is robust: maximizing worst-case outperformance relative to the benchmark model. Finally, we select the Pareto optimal model with maximum (out-of-sample) expected utility. We show that our method reduces to the minimum relative entropy method if and only if the utility function is a member of a three-parameter logarithmic family.

findings.summary: The derivation drops nonnegativity constraints that affect the solution. The proposed learning family can contain no feasible model even when the original calibration problem has a feasible solution.
findings.claim: Theorem 1 and the main non-logarithmic computational representation: the primal calibration problem and feature-dimensional regularized expected-utility dual have the same unique probability model for every allowed utility and interior tolerance.

For allowed square-root utility, the resulting connecting family contains no feasible model for a strictly feasible calibration problem with all-positive data/prior and interior alpha.

Alpha40/13 is interior to [0,2560/13] and requires mean q1+2q2 between .1 and .3; the all-positive empirical model is strictly feasible. Every positive q satisfies Assumption 1 with lambda=||q|| and bets q²/||q||². Connecting-family equations preserve n·U for n=(1,−2,1), hence require sign(1−3q_middle)=sign(1−3*.98)<0. Every feasible q has q_middle<=.3, giving the opposite positive sign. Thus no advertised-family model is feasible, even with limits/strictly positive interpretation. Unique closed-simplex primal optimum(.7,.3,0) has essential nu2=2/sqrt58+388/sqrt9606≈4.22138 and uncorrected G2=−2−nu2 below the inverse domain. Restoring active nonnegativity constraints changes the advertised connecting family; alternatively, additional utility restrictions exclude the allowed power range 0<kappa<1. A constant rescaling or endpoint correction cannot repair an empty feasible intersection. The valid convex primal and logarithmic special case do not establish the claimed general-utility computational contribution.

papers.title: Optimality of Universal Bayesian Sequence Prediction for General Loss and Alphabet
papers.abstract: Various optimality properties of universal sequence predictors based on Bayes-mixtures in general, and Solomonoff's prediction scheme in particular, will be studied. The probability of observing xt at time t, given past observations x1...xt-1 can be computed with the chain rule if the true generating distribution μ of the sequences x1x2x3.... is known. If μ is unknown, but known to belong to a countable or continuous class Μ one can base ones prediction on the Bayes-mixture ξ defined as a wν-weighted sum or integral of distributions ν ∈ Μ. The cumulative expected loss of the Bayes-optimal universal prediction scheme based on ξ is shown to be close to the loss of the Bayes-optimal, but infeasible prediction scheme based on μ. We show that the bounds are tight and that no other predictor can lead to significantly smaller bounds. Furthermore, for various performance measures, we show Pareto-optimality of ξ and give an Occam's razor argument that the choice wν &sim 2-K(ν) for the weights is optimal, where K(ν) is the length of the shortest program describing ν. The results are applied to games of chance, defined as a sequence of bets, observations, and rewards. The prediction schemes (and bounds) are compared to the popular predictors based on expert advice. Extensions to infinite alphabets, partial, delayed and probabilistic prediction, classification, and more active systems are briefly discussed.

findings.summary: An allowed smooth model family has prediction regret that grows linearly rather than logarithmically. This defeats the advertised extension of the prediction guarantee to continuous model classes.
findings.claim: The continuous-class Fisher-information entropy bound and its resulting near-optimal bounded-loss Bayesian prediction guarantee under the printed inverse-information equicontinuity assumptions.
findings.location: PDF page 23 (printed 993), Theorem 8 and proof; PDF page 24 (printed 994), continuous-class prediction extension; abstract and PDF pages 3/27 state the affected contribution.
findings.explanation: A C2, strictly positive eight-symbol continuous family with interior true parameter and equicontinuous bounded inverse mean Fisher information has D_n=Omega(n), rather than the asserted O(log n), and bounded quadratic-loss regret Omega(n).
findings.evidence: X_t=(A_t,B_t,Y_t), independent Bernoulli coordinates with pA=.5+.25sin(t theta), pB=.5+.25cos(t theta), pY=.25+.5g(exp(t)theta), theta in[-1,1], uniform prior, theta0=0, C2 compact transition g. jbar_n(0)=(n+1)(2n+1)/24; inverse uniformly <=24/((n+1)(2n+1)) and equicontinuous. For n divisible by12, E={sumY<=n/3}: mu(E)>=1-exp(-n/72), xi(E)<=exp(-n/4)+exp(-121n/864). Therefore D_n>=(1-exp(-n/72))*(121n/864-log2)-log2=Omega(n), against 1.5log n+O(1)+o(1). All conditional symbol probabilities>=1/64 imply D_n<=64S_n and bounded Brier regret=S_n/2>=D_n/128. At n1200 the analytic lower166.669 and displayed main RHS9.1675 illustrate scale; asymptotic separation handles unspecified o(1).
findings.impact: The abstract expressly covers continuous classes and Theorem8 is the sole support for that extension. An admitted smooth family gives a positive average bounded-loss gap, overturning the stated near-optimal continuous prediction conclusion. Adequate uniform local-KL hypotheses/proof and a restricted class are needed; constant changes cannot repair it. Replacing inverse by information continuity excludes this witness and is not itself disproved here. Discrete and ordinary regular IID results are not refuted.

papers.title: Blind Source Recovery: A Framework in the State Space
papers.abstract: Blind Source Recovery (BSR) denotes recovery of original sources/signals from environments that may include convolution, temporal variation, and even nonlinearity. It also infers the recovery of sources even in the absence of precise environment identifiability. This paper describes, in a comprehensive fashion, a generalized BSR formulation achieved by the application of stochastic optimization principles to the Kullback-Liebler divergence as a performance functional subject to the constraints of the general (i.e., nonlinear and time-varying) state space representation. This technique is used to derive update laws for nonlinear time-varying dynamical systems, which are subsequently specialized to time-invariant and linear systems. Further, the state space demixing network structures have been exploited to develop learning rules, capable of handling most filtering paradigms, which can be conveniently extended to nonlinear models. In the special cases, distinct linear state-space algorithms are presented for the minimum phase and non-minimum phase mixing environment models. Conventional (FIR/IIR) filtering models are subsequently derived from this general structure and are compared with material in the recent literature. Illustrative simulation examples are presented to demonstrate the online adaptation capabilities of the developed algorithms. Some of this reported work has also been implemented in dedicated hardware/software platforms.

findings.summary: The proposed independence gradient can move away from the correct separation of temporal sources. In an allowed Gaussian example, it loses a true component instead of recovering it.
findings.claim: Theorem3.1 is the natural gradient of the stated instantaneous output mutual information and supports source recovery up to permutation/scale/delay under signal independence alone.
findings.location: PDF p2 (printed 1412), independence-only source scope; p4 (1414), Eq1 single-tap recovery; pp5–6 (1415–16), Eqs2–4 instantaneous MI; p10 (1420), Eqs27–29; p11 (1421), Theorem3.1 Eqs30–31; pp13–14 (1423–24), Eqs41–42; p25 (1435), Eq97; p26 (1436), Eq98.
findings.explanation: An admissible colored Gaussian MA source with stable minimum-phase whitening mixing has iid observations. At its exact inverse, MI is identically zero along all nearby diagonal demixers but Eq30 has drift -eta/sqrt5. The available Gaussian-score population dynamics erase the true temporal component and increase printed ISI from 0 toward 2.
findings.evidence: rho=1/2,b=sqrt5/2,s1=(epsilon_t+rho epsilon_(t-1))/b, independent unit-variance iid logistic s2; Hbar=diag(b/(1+rho z^-1),1); observations iid. Exact inverse C11=1/sqrt5,D11=2/sqrt5,A=0,B=I. Ephi(y)y^T=I, Ephi(y)X^T=diag(1/sqrt5,0), yielding nonzero claimed gradient despite MI=0. Gaussian-branch ODE c/d=.5e^-t, d^-2=1+.25(1+2t)e^-2t, with ISI=2(1-e^-t). Wrong identity satisfies auxiliary score conditions but cannot equal source up to a single tap, because lag1correlations are 0 and2/5.
findings.impact: Foundational gradient and broad independence-only single-tap recovery fail. Repair requires changing the objective/temporal source scope or recovery target, rather than a local parameter/constant correction. Historical table/trajectory results are not claimed false.

papers.title: Rational Kernels: Theory and Algorithms
papers.abstract: Many classification algorithms were originally designed for fixed-size vectors. Recent applications in text and speech processing and computational biology require however the analysis of variable-length sequences and more generally weighted automata. An approach widely used in statistical learning techniques such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs) is that of kernel methods, due to their computational efficiency in high-dimensional feature spaces. We introduce a general family of kernels based on weighted transducers or rational relations, rational kernels , that extend kernel methods to the analysis of variable-length sequences or more generally weighted automata. We show that rational kernels can be computed efficiently using a general algorithm of composition of weighted transducers and a general single-source shortest-distance algorithm. Not all rational kernels are positive definite and symmetric (PDS), or equivalently verify the Mercer condition, a condition that guarantees the convergence of training for discriminant classification algorithms such as SVMs. We present several theoretical results related to PDS rational kernels. We show that under some general conditions these kernels are closed under sum, product, or Kleene-closure and give a general method for constructing a PDS rational kernel from an arbitrary transducer defined on some non-idempotent semirings. We give the proof of several characterization results that can be used to guide the design of PDS rational kernels. We also show that some commonly used string kernels or similarity measures such as the edit-distance, the convolution kernels of Haussler, and some string kernels used in the context of computational biology are specific instances of rational kernels. Our results include the proof that the edit-distance over a non-trivial alphabet is not negative definite, which, to the best of our knowledge, was never stated or proved before. Rational kernels can be combined with SVMs to form efficient and powerful techniques for a variety of classification tasks in text and speech processing, or computational biology. We describe examples of general families of PDS rational kernels that are useful in many of these applications and report the result of our experiments illustrating the use of rational kernels in several difficult large-vocabulary spoken-dialog classification tasks based on deployed spoken-dialog systems. Our results show that rational kernels are easy to design and implement and lead to substantial improvements of the classification accuracy.

findings.summary: The proof confuses nonnegative diagonal entries with nonnegative entries throughout a matrix. A valid rational kernel lacks the required factorization, contradicting the claimed characterization.
findings.claim: The advertised acyclic characterization: every acyclic PDS rational kernel admits an equivalent T composed with its inverse, with T over the nonnegative probability semiring; the accompanying proposed general nonnegative-factor characterization.
findings.location: Proposition 8, PDF page 11 (printed 1045), Cholesky proof on PDF page 12 (printed 1046), and characterization discussion following Proposition 9 on PDF page 13 (printed 1047). Probability semiring: Table 1, PDF page 3.
findings.explanation: The nonnegative SPD matrix I + (3/5) A(C5) is a PDS rational kernel of an explicit acyclic probability-semiring transducer but has no nonnegative Gram factor. The proof confuses a Cholesky factor with nonnegative diagonal with an entrywise nonnegative factor.
findings.evidence: Let x_i=a^i for i=1,...,5 and K(x_i,x_j)=M_ij, zero elsewhere, where M=I+(3/5)A(C5). Its eigenvalues are 11/5 and (7±3sqrt(5))/10 twice each, all strictly positive. A separate successful path for each nonzero M_ij realizes K using only nonnegative weights. If M_ij=sum_z v_i(z)v_j(z) with all v_i(z)>=0, zero nonedges force each column support into a clique of C5, hence at most two adjacent coordinates. Per column sum_i v_i^2>=2sum_cycle_edges v_i v_j. Summing requires trace M=5>=2sum_cycle_edges M_ij=6, a contradiction. The exact checker confirms every supported and unsupported input/output length through six.
findings.impact: The abstract, introduction and section outline advertise a characterization, with the acyclic case specifically presented as proved. This counterexample invalidates that necessity result within the claimed nonnegative representation class and refutes the proposed extension already in its established finite base case. A complete-positivity restriction or a change to signed factors is required; PDS alone does not characterize the stated class. Signed real Cholesky factors would prove a different representation result, not restore the asserted nonnegative characterization. The sufficient Gram construction, edit-distance result, practical expected-count kernels and classification experiments are not refuted.

papers.title: The Minimum Error Minimax Probability Machine
papers.abstract: We construct a distribution-free Bayes optimal classifier called the Minimum Error Minimax Probability Machine (MEMPM) in a worst-case setting, i.e., under all possible choices of class-conditional densities with a given mean and covariance matrix. By assuming no specific distributions for the data, our model is thus distinguished from traditional Bayes optimal approaches, where an assumption on the data distribution is a must. This model is extended from the Minimax Probability Machine (MPM), a recently-proposed novel classifier, and is demonstrated to be the general case of MPM. Moreover, it includes another special case named the Biased Minimax Probability Machine, which is appropriate for handling biased classification. One appealing feature of MEMPM is that it contains an explicit performance indicator, i.e., a lower bound on the worst-case accuracy, which is shown to be tighter than that of MPM. We provide conditions under which the worst-case Bayes optimal classifier converges to the Bayes optimal classifier. We demonstrate how to apply a more general statistical framework to estimate model input parameters robustly. We also show how to extend our model to nonlinear classification by exploiting kernelization techniques. A series of experiments on both synthetic data sets and real world benchmark data sets validates our proposition and demonstrates the effectiveness of our model.

findings.summary: Reformulated probability constraints exclude thresholds allowed by the original problem. The proposed minimum-error solver can miss better permitted solutions and does not solve the stated problem generally.
findings.claim: The sequential MEMPM optimization exactly solves the unrestricted expected worst-case error minimization over all finite intercepts and nonzero hyperplane normals.
findings.location: PDF p3 (journal p1255), Eq1–3; PDF p6 (p1258), Lemma1 and Eq4–7; PDF pp7–8 (pp1259–1260), Eq9–15. Application consequence: PDF p21 (p1273), Pima rows of Tables2–3.

findings.claim: The stated component-wise Lyapunov condition suffices for the Gaussian-CDF MEMPM hyperplane to converge to the true Bayes optimal hyperplane in high dimensions.
findings.location: PDF p10 (journal p1262), Theorem5 and the subsequent weighted-projection deduction; PDF p11 (p1263), Proposition6. Advertised in abstract and conclusion PDF p32.
