papers.title: Subgroup Discovery with CN2-SD
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how to adapt standard classification rule learning approaches to subgroup discovery. The goal of subgroup discovery is to find rules describing subsets of the population that are sufficiently large and statistically unusual. The paper presents a subgroup discovery algorithm, CN2-SD, developed by modifying parts of the CN2 classification rule learner: its covering algorithm, search heuristic, probabilistic classification of instances, and evaluation measures. Experimental evaluation of CN2-SD on 23 UCI data sets shows substantial reduction of the number of induced rules, increased rule coverage and rule significance, as well as slight improvements in terms of the area under ROC curve, when compared with the CN2 algorithm. Application of CN2-SD to a large traffic accident data set confirms these findings.

findings.summary: Reported subgroup scores and coverage values exceed mathematical bounds, while accuracy and AUC entries conflict with the stated prediction rule. These conflicts undermine the reported empirical validation.
findings.claim: The comparative evaluation establishes improved fixed-population subgroup quality, principally average WRAcc, with increased coverage and maintained or improved predictive performance. The impossible detailed metrics feed the summary comparisons and substantive interpretations.
findings.location: Equation (1), PDF page 5; Sections 4.1 and 5.1, PDF pages 10 and 13–14; Tables 3 and 18, PDF pages 16 and 31, hypothyroid row 10. Corroboration: Table 14, PDF page 27, echo and wine; Tables 19–20 and Figure 3, PDF pages 32–33 and 12, Australian and vote; common classifier definitions in Sections 2.3, 3.3 and 4.2.2.
findings.explanation: Reported fixed-population WRAcc on hypothyroid exceeds its exact class-prior-dependent maximum under every stated averaging scheme. Several mean coverages exceed one. Independently, several accuracy/AUC pairs are incompatible with the explicitly shared thresholded-posterior classifier.
findings.evidence: Hypothyroid has N = 3163 and reported majority 95%. Even allowing majority only 94%, every stratified test fold has majority fraction at least 297/317 and every rule or average has |WRACC| <= 5940/100489 = 0.05911094747. Table 18 reports 0.067, 0.076, 0.073, 0.076 and 0.072 for the five nonstandard methods; the smallest rounding-compatible 0.0665 still exceeds the bound. Full/training population bounds are tighter. Weighted search scores are distinct from the fixed-population evaluation explicitly defined in Section 5.1. COV = mean n(Cond)/N cannot exceed one but four cells do. The common posterior definition also requires AUC >= (ACC-m)/(1-m); conservative Australian and vote bounds contradict Table 20. No common cause, corrected ranking or failure of every result is inferred.
findings.impact: The paper principally validates its subgroup-discovery modification through comparative empirical quality gains. Its explicitly preferred subgroup-quality metric and supporting evaluation values cannot arise under its stated definitions and protocol. A residual-weight or balanced-population reinterpretation changes the metric and requires a redefined or recalculated comparative evaluation; changing the AUC score likewise changes the stated prediction comparison. This invalid central evaluation record cannot support the claimed gains/significance as written. The weighted-covering idea and valid WRAcc algebra are not refuted, and no corrected ranking is asserted.

papers.title: A Compression Approach to Support Vector Model Selection
papers.abstract: In this paper we investigate connections between statistical learning theory and data compression on the basis of support vector machine (SVM) model selection. Inspired by several generalization bounds we construct "compression coefficients" for SVMs which measure the amount by which the training labels can be compressed by a code built from the separating hyperplane. The main idea is to relate the coding precision to geometrical concepts such as the width of the margin or the shape of the data in the feature space. The so derived compression coefficients combine well known quantities such as the radius-margin term R2/ρ2, the eigenvalues of the kernel matrix, and the number of support vectors. To test whether they are useful in practice we ran model selection experiments on benchmark data sets. As a result we found that compression coefficients can fairly accurately predict the parameters for which the test error is minimized.

findings.summary: The proposed label code has too few messages to distinguish all permitted labelings. This breaks the coding criterion and the generalization argument built on that code.
findings.claim: The favored ellipsoid-based compression coefficient is the bit length of an actual training-label code, providing a theoretical justification for SVM model selection.
findings.location: PDF page 10 (printed 302), Code 2 and C2 formula; PDF page 7 (printed 299), exception definition; PDF pages 4–5 and 9, rotation geometry. Main contribution framing: PDF pages 1, 3 and 24.
findings.explanation: The claimed message is not capable of transmitting the labels. On fixed centered inputs, 2^256 soft-margin SVM labelings have the same margin, spectrum, r=4, l=0 and fixed exception fields, but the codeword index has only 128 choices. No choice of cover or decoder can repair the claimed C2 message.
findings.evidence: For m=516, inputs are ±e_i/16 for i=1,...,256 with arbitrary opposite labels ±b_i, plus four fixed far observations ±16e_257 labeled +,- at each endpoint. At C=1 all alpha=1, w=(b/8,0), primal=dual514, norm2, rho1/2 and R16. The positive spectrum is 1024 once and 1/128 repeated256, so n128. All 512 small points are outside the rotation cone and correctly labeled; r4 far exceptions and their labels are fixed, l0. Only seven varying index bits must identify 256 arbitrary label bits. Even all claimed bit fields rounded up total84<256. A valid 128-ball ellipsoid cover has radius at most sqrt(9/128)<1/2 and fails every small pair. The distinct/separable variant gives the same n/r/l/spectrum and 2^254 labelings.
findings.impact: Actual label coding and its generalization justification are explicit central contributions, and C2 is the preferred new criterion. The counterexample disproves that claimed operational meaning. Correcting the exception set to the full margin strip or normalizing rows changes the coefficient and the information budget; the same short code is impossible. Surviving heuristic usefulness and valid other codes do not restore the paper’s central theoretical contribution as written.

papers.title: Distributional Scaling: An Algorithm for Structure-Preserving Embedding of Metric and Nonmetric Spaces
papers.abstract: We present a novel approach for embedding general metric and nonmetric spaces into low-dimensional Euclidean spaces. As opposed to traditional multidimensional scaling techniques, which minimize the distortion of pairwise distances, our embedding algorithm seeks a low-dimensional representation of the data that preserves the structure (geometry) of the original data. The algorithm uses a hybrid criterion function that combines the pairwise distortion with what we call the geometric distortion. To assess the geometric distortion, we explore functions that reflect geometric properties. Our approach is different from the Isomap and LLE algorithms in that the discrepancy in distributional information is used to guide the embedding. We use clustering algorithms in conjunction with our embedding algorithm to direct the embedding process and improve its convergence properties. We test our method on metric and nonmetric data sets, and in the presence of noise. We demonstrate that our method preserves the structural properties of embedded data better than traditional MDS, and that its performance is robust with respect to clustering errors in the original data. Other results of the paper include accelerated algorithms for optimizing the standard MDS objective functions, and two methods for finding the most appropriate dimension in which to embed a given set of data.

findings.summary: The dimension-selection proof treats boundary geometry as a linear space. The resulting reference distribution and significance calibration fail, undermining the proposed statistical decision rule.
findings.claim: Under small distortions at a locally optimal p-dimensional embedding and an isotropically oriented normal-space residual, increasing to dimension q removes a fixed linear collection of residual coordinates, yielding F=s(q)/s(p)=A/(A+B) with independent chi-squared A and B and calibrated significance for choosing dimension.
findings.location: Section 2.8.1, PDF pages 18–20 (journal pages 416–418), especially the last paragraph of page 416 and the normal-space projection and chi-squared ratio on page 417; Section 3.2, PDF pages 22–24 and Table 2 apply the significance rule.
findings.explanation: A rank-p distance configuration is a singular boundary point of the q-dimensional distance set. Added coordinates create a cone of quadratic directions, rather than the fixed linear subspace assumed by the null-law derivation. The claimed beta null and corresponding dimension-selection calibration fail even as distortions tend to zero.
findings.evidence: For n=4,p=1,q=2 at coordinates 0,1,2,3, the three outward triangle normals span the normal space. Every positive combination R gives target D0+epsilon*R whose globally nearest Euclidean distance vector in every dimension is D0, so F=1. A spherical cap of null probability at least 1/44 lies in this cone for every sufficiently small epsilon; the predicted Beta(1/2,1) has no atom at 1. Separately, for the 64 vertices of the 6D cube with sigma=1e-6, 100 fresh uniform normal directions and explicitly stored feasible 7D embeddings, the claimed exact beta calculation gives 44 nominal p-values <=.0025 and the printed normal approximation gives 60. The 6D base remains a strict local minimum modulo Euclidean motions; no global 7D optimality is assumed. Independent recomputation changes ratios by at most 1.33e-9. Historical Table 2 values are not claimed incorrect.
findings.impact: Quantitative dimension selection is an expressly advertised contribution, distinguished from the heuristic alternative and used to produce Table 2. Its indispensable statistical null and significance certificate are false even under the stated normal-orientation model and arbitrarily small distortions. Repair requires a configuration-dependent cone/optimization law or a different calibrated procedure, not a local constant, sign or degree-of-freedom correction. Separate distributional-objective gains, majorizers, MDL heuristic and historical experiments are not asserted false.

papers.title: Efficient Feature Selection via Analysis of Relevance and Redundancy
papers.abstract: Feature selection is applied to reduce the number of features in many applications where data has hundreds or thousands of features. Existing feature selection methods mainly focus on finding relevant features. In this paper, we show that feature relevance alone is insufficient for efficient feature selection of high-dimensional data. We define feature redundancy and propose to perform explicit redundancy analysis in feature selection. A new framework is introduced that decouples relevance analysis and redundancy analysis. We develop a correlation-based method for relevance and redundancy analysis, and conduct an empirical study of its efficiency and effectiveness comparing with representative methods.

findings.summary: Feature selection and discretization use test-fold labels before cross-validation. The prediction evaluation includes information from the examples it is supposed to hold out.
findings.claim: FCBF preserves or improves prediction accuracy on novel cases, as supported by cross-validated benchmark comparisons.
findings.location: Section 5.3.1, PDF pages 13–14 (journal pages 1217–1218), full-data selection followed by classifier cross-validation; Section 5.3.2, PDF page 15, inherits that protocol. Central accuracy Tables 5–6 and 10–11; Table 10 on PDF page 17. Sections 5.4 and 6 draw predictive conclusions.
findings.explanation: Supervised feature selection and MDL discretization use all labels before classifier cross-validation, so held-out labels influence the selected feature set and preprocessing. The claimed validation is not independent.
findings.evidence: For 12 balanced labels and 8192 independent fair-bit null columns, a perfect matching/complement column exists with probability 1−(1−1/2048)^8192 = 0.9817022445654648. FCBF(0) retains one such column, giving 100% leaked validation versus exactly 50% future accuracy. Primary Arcene data plus a modern primary-source-guided translation selects the published 39/24 features. Raw Gaussian NBC gives default 93% leaked CV versus 70% properly nested CV and 65% independent validation; log2 gives 93%/72%/65%. Full-feature scores are 70% CV and 72% validation. The default 39-feature/93% match corroborates the reconstruction; the log and full scores differ from the historical table, so no authenticated exact historical rerun is claimed. Both raw numeric and discretized classifier paths show substantial gaps.
findings.impact: Predictive effectiveness is a central empirical contribution. Every reported benchmark accuracy comparison uses supervised information from cases subsequently treated as held out. The protocol can produce perfect apparent validation from wholly uninformative features, and controlled Arcene checks remove the large apparent default gain. Repair requires new evaluations and significance comparisons, so the central predictive evidence cannot be retained as written. The algorithm heuristic and timing results are not independently refuted.

papers.title: A Fast Algorithm for Joint Diagonalization with Non-orthogonal Transformations and its Application to Blind Source Separation
papers.abstract: A new efficient algorithm is presented for joint diagonalization of several matrices. The algorithm is based on the Frobenius-norm formulation of the joint diagonalization problem, and addresses diagonalization with a general, non-orthogonal transformation. The iterative scheme of the algorithm is based on a multiplicative update which ensures the invertibility of the diagonalizer. The algorithm's efficiency stems from the special approximation of the cost function resulting in a sparse, block-diagonal Hessian to be used in the computation of the quasi-Newton update step. Extensive numerical simulations illustrate the performance of the algorithm and provide a comparison to other leading diagonalization methods. The results of such comparison demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is a viable alternative to existing state-of-the-art joint diagonalization algorithms. The practical use of our algorithm is shown for blind source separation problems.

findings.summary: Permitted updates can shrink every factor toward zero rather than solve the separation problem. A decreasing objective does not establish the advertised avoidance of trivial solutions.
findings.claim: The defining multiplicative invertibility safeguard guarantees avoidance of the trivial zero solution for general real symmetric joint approximate diagonalization without orthogonality or positive-definiteness assumptions.
findings.location: PDF page 4 (printed 780), contribution bullet and Section 2; PDF pages 5–6 (printed 781–782), Equations (7)–(9) and Algorithm 1; PDF page 8 (printed 784), Equation (17).
findings.explanation: For every positive step cap, three allowed symmetric 2×2 matrices give an exact alternating update cycle whose two-step product is a scalar contraction. All finite iterates are invertible and all block denominators are positive, yet V tends to zero and the raw objective decays entirely by scale shrinkage.
findings.evidence: For 0<a<min(theta/sqrt(2),1/sqrt(2)), set C1=[[1,-2a],[-2a,1]], C2=[[0,sqrt(1-2a²)],[sqrt(1-2a²),0]], C3=diag(1,-1). Equation17 gives W0=aX and W1=-aX, with denominators4 and4(1-a²)^4. Both ||W||F=sqrt(2)a<theta. Since (I-aX)(I+aX)=(1-a²)I, V_2t=(1-a²)^tI tends tozero. F_n=(1-a²)^(2n)F0 decreases at every step; even-iterate relative off-norm remains (1+2a²)/(3+2a²). A=.25,theta=.5 yields V norm1.37e-14 after1000updates. Exact scripts and results under checks/2004__accepted__v5-ziehe04a.
findings.impact: Avoiding the trivial solution is an expressly advertised defining feature and the stated reason the otherwise degenerate non-orthogonal Frobenius formulation is usable. The published safeguard fails on allowed approximate problems while all its checks succeed, permitting arbitrarily small apparent error without relative diagonalization improvement. Repair requires an explicit new treatment of scale in algorithm and analysis or a material scope restriction. Later normalization can restore avoidance but changes the published recurrence; no global convergence promise or falsity of successful exact examples is asserted.

papers.title: Clustering with Bregman Divergences
papers.abstract: A wide variety of distortion functions, such as squared Euclidean distance, Mahalanobis distance, Itakura-Saito distance and relative entropy, have been used for clustering. In this paper, we propose and analyze parametric hard and soft clustering algorithms based on a large class of distortion functions known as Bregman divergences. The proposed algorithms unify centroid-based parametric clustering approaches, such as classical kmeans, the Linde-Buzo-Gray (LBG) algorithm and information-theoretic clustering, which arise by special choices of the Bregman divergence. The algorithms maintain the simplicity and scalability of the classical kmeans algorithm, while generalizing the method to a large class of clustering loss functions. This is achieved by first posing the hard clustering problem in terms of minimizing the loss in Bregman information, a quantity motivated by rate distortion theory, and then deriving an iterative algorithm that monotonically decreases this loss. In addition, we show that there is a bijection between regular exponential families and a large class of Bregman divergences, that we call regular Bregman divergences. This result enables the development of an alternative interpretation of an efficient EM scheme for learning mixtures of exponential family distributions, and leads to a simple soft clustering algorithm for regular Bregman divergences. Finally, we discuss the connection between rate distortion theory and Bregman clustering and present an information theoretic analysis of Bregman clustering algorithms in terms of a trade-off between compression and loss in Bregman information.

findings.summary: The claimed likelihood family may not exist for a permitted scaling of the divergence. Normalizing it changes the optimizer, breaking the proposed general equivalence between clustering and likelihood estimation.
findings.claim: Finite-cardinality rate-distortion optimization with arbitrary regular Bregman divergence and positive variational scale is equivalent to maximum-likelihood estimation in a corresponding exponential family.
findings.location: PDF page 30 (printed 1734), Theorems 7–8 and the likelihood interpretation of Eq. 23; PDF page 32 (printed 1736), the unrestricted multinomial mixture interpretation; contribution 6 on PDF page 3.
findings.explanation: Fractionally scaling a regular Bregman divergence can require a cumulant with a negative even central moment, so the asserted likelihood family does not exist. Normalizing powered densities adds a parameter-dependent term and changes the optimizer.
findings.evidence: For Bernoulli KL and beta=1/2, the required cumulant is beta log(1+exp(theta/beta)); its centered MGF sqrt(cosh t) has fourth central moment -1/4. The literally printed beta*psi interpretation gives -1/64. Beta=3/2 yields tenth central moments -2039/629856 (required scaling) and -6117/32768 (literal). For data 0001, k=1, the RDFC centroid is q=1/4 but the normalized square-root-powered Bernoulli model has ML q=1/10. Choosing tolerated distortion H(1/4) makes every positive beta an optimal Lagrange multiplier, satisfying that interpretation of the theorem.
findings.impact: The general ML/rate-distortion equivalence is an explicit main contribution. Its target distribution can fail to exist even for the elementary Bernoulli example, and the direct normalization repair changes the objective and M-step. A substantive restriction to admissible scales/families or withdrawal of the likelihood interpretation is required. The energy/BA identity and valid hard-clustering results are preserved in the report.

papers.title: A Bayesian Model for Supervised Clustering with the Dirichlet Process Prior
papers.abstract: We develop a Bayesian framework for tackling the supervised clustering problem, the generic problem encountered in tasks such as reference matching, coreference resolution, identity uncertainty and record linkage. Our clustering model is based on the Dirichlet process prior, which enables us to define distributions over the countably infinite sets that naturally arise in this problem. We add supervision to our model by positing the existence of a set of unobserved random variables (we call these "reference types") that are generic across all clusters. Inference in our framework, which requires integrating over infinitely many parameters, is solved using Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques. We present algorithms for both conjugate and non-conjugate priors. We present a simple---but general---parameterization of our model based on a Gaussian assumption. We evaluate this model on one artificial task and three real-world tasks, comparing it against both unsupervised and state-of-the-art supervised algorithms. Our results show that our model is able to outperform other models across a variety of tasks and performance metrics.

findings.summary: A reused conditional density omits a normalization term that depends on the parameters. The proposed Bayesian sampler can consequently target a distribution that cannot be normalized.
findings.claim: The nonconjugate SCDP-3 procedure performs posterior inference for the stated precision-given-means model and supports its full Bayesian interpretation.
findings.location: Section 5.2, Equation (3), PDF page 10 (journal 1560), and mean-proposal weighting paragraph on PDF page 11 (journal 1561); SCDP-3 experiments in Section 7 and full-Bayesian claim on PDF page 20.
findings.explanation: The precision conditional has a mean-dependent normalizer. Its unnormalized kernel is reused for mean proposals, changing the target; an allowed Gaussian/gamma example gives a nonnormalizable mean and joint target.
findings.evidence: K=2,L=1, Gp=N(0,1), Gt=Gamma(1,1), class sizes2/1 and distinct observations(-sqrt(3/2),+sqrt(3/2),0). Eq3 kernel R=g(p1)^(-2)exp(-(1+(p1-p2)^2)tau) has Z=g(p1)^(-2)/(1+(p1-p2)^2). Correct normalized model gives p1 conditional (1+p1^2)exp(-.7p1^2) at p2=0,tau=.1; printed proposal times kernel and likelihood gives exp(+.3p1^2), not integrable. A positive-measure joint region yields lower bound C exp(p1^2/2)p1^(-5), also divergent. Correct conditional model has finite evidence.
findings.impact: SCDP-3 is the strongest proposed separation model and supports the headline comparisons and full-Bayesian nonconjugate claim. Repair changes the substantive mean/partition target and cancels the explicitly used mean-prior/order factors; MH mechanics or additional samples cannot fix the same target. A proper normalized model exists and the gamma normalizer is elementary, but the central claimed inference procedure is not Bayesian for it as written. No historical implementation or score error is inferred; SCDP1/2 survive.

papers.title: Concentration Bounds for Unigram Language Models
papers.abstract: We show several high-probability concentration bounds for learning unigram language models. One interesting quantity is the probability of all words appearing exactly k times in a sample of size m. A standard estimator for this quantity is the Good-Turing estimator. The existing analysis on its error shows a high-probability bound of approximately O(k / m1/2). We improve its dependency on k to O(k1/4 / m1/2 + k / m). We also analyze the empirical frequencies estimator, showing that with high probability its error is bounded by approximately O( 1 / k + k1/2 / m). We derive a combined estimator, which has an error of approximately O(m-2/5), for any k. A standard measure for the quality of a learning algorithm is its expected per-word log-loss. The leave-one-out method can be used for estimating the log-loss of the unigram model. We show that its error has a high-probability bound of approximately O(1 / m1/2), for any underlying distribution. We also bound the log-loss a priori, as a function of various parameters of the distribution.

findings.summary: The bound omits uncertainty contributed by many rare words. An explicit distribution violates the advertised high-confidence guarantee, so the certificate can understate language-model prediction loss.
findings.claim: A priori high-probability KL log-loss upper bound and its distribution-cutoff characterization for the absolute-discounting unigram estimator.
findings.location: PDF page 21 (printed 1251), Theorem 39; PDF pages 22–23, Lemma 41 and Equation (28); Appendix A.4, PDF pages 32–33.
findings.explanation: The bound omits sampling loss among many below-cutoff words because signed denominator/probability comparisons are invalid. An explicit finite positive distribution has KL > 1.3e-5 while the theorem RHS < 7.5e-7 with probability > .9999998, although delta = .1.
findings.evidence: B=10^16 bulk words, r=148, m=rB, R=isqrt(m)=1216552506 rare words. Bulk p=(m-R)/(mB), rare p=1/m; alpha=1/m,tau=1,lambda=4,delta=.1. All probabilities are below the theorem cutoff. With probability at least 1-128/R-128/R²-B exp(-(r-R/B))-exp(-m/(128r)) > .9999998947, every bulk word occurs, rare n0,n1 >=R/8, and bulk empirical L1 deviation >=1/(8sqrt(r)). Q is normalized and strictly positive. Discounting perturbs bulk L1 by at most B/m², so Pinsker gives KL >=1/(512r)=.00001319679. Exact Theorem39 RHS <=.0000007452061. The corresponding B→infinity family has actual lower bound Omega(1/ln B) versus claimed O(ln m/sqrt m), so no constant adjustment repairs it.
findings.impact: The false a priori log-loss theorem is an expressly advertised main contribution and underlies the paper's characterization of which distributions are easy to learn. Restoring valid signs requires an additional sampling contribution or a different analysis of the below-cutoff population, not a typographical constant change. The separate Good–Turing and leave-one-out rates are not claimed refuted.

papers.title: New Horn Revision Algorithms
papers.abstract: A revision algorithm is a learning algorithm that identifies the target concept, starting from an initial concept. Such an algorithm is considered efficient if its complexity (in terms of the measured resource) is polynomial in the syntactic distance between the initial and the target concept, but only polylogarithmic in the number of variables in the universe. We give efficient revision algorithms in the model of learning with equivalence and membership queries. The algorithms work in a general revision model where both deletion and addition revision operators are allowed. In this model one of the main open problems is the efficient revision of Horn formulas. Two revision algorithms are presented for special cases of this problem: for depth-1 acyclic Horn formulas, and for definite Horn formulas with unique heads.

findings.summary: The algorithm never lets initial rule heads become body variables. It misses target cases that the claimed procedure is supposed to handle after changing rule heads.
findings.claim: Correct efficient revision of all stated depth-1 acyclic Horn formulas under both head deletion and body addition, the first of the two main algorithmic contributions.
findings.location: PDF pages 7–10 (printed 1925–1928), initial-head convention, Proposition 1, Algorithm 2 lines 16 and 27–37, Lemma 1; Lemma 3 on pages 10–12 and Theorem 5 on page 13. Allowed edits: page 6, explicit head-deletion distance: page 11.
findings.explanation: The algorithm permanently treats initial heads as unavailable body variables. A permitted deletion of a head followed by its addition to a target body makes Proposition 1 false; Algorithm 2 strips the necessary variable and permanently excludes a target-positive assignment.
findings.evidence: Initial (a→b)∧(c→d); target (a→F)∧(b∧c→d), exact distance2. Initial, intermediate and target graphs all have depth1. First legal EQ counterexample0110 gives head d and negative new0110; line36 removes b and adds c→d, which rejects target-positive0010. All subsequent operations strengthen H, so this valid instance can never be learned for any larger budget or subsequent EQ choices. No binary search or pivot is invoked.
findings.impact: An entire advertised algorithm fails on the head-changing cases it claims to add beyond previous restricted work. The invariant, structural proposition and body construction all fail, and future updates cannot repair the excluded target-positive assignment. Fixing local pseudocode typos does not restore correctness; imposing a common head/body partition materially narrows the main claimed result. This does not refute the existence of other algorithms or the separate definite unique-head contribution.

papers.title: Generalization Bounds and Complexities Based on Sparsity and Clustering for Convex Combinations of Functions from Random Classes
papers.abstract: A unified approach is taken for deriving new generalization data dependent bounds for several classes of algorithms explored in the existing literature by different approaches. This unified approach is based on an extension of Vapnik's inequality for VC classes of sets to random classes of sets - that is, classes depending on the random data, invariant under permutation of the data and possessing the increasing property. Generalization bounds are derived for convex combinations of functions from random classes with certain properties. Algorithms, such as SVMs (support vector machines), boosting with decision stumps, radial basis function networks, some hierarchies of kernel machines or convex combinations of indicator functions over sets with finite VC dimension, generate classifier functions that fall into the above category. We also explore the individual complexities of the classifiers, such as sparsity of weights and weighted variance over clusters from the convex combination introduced by Koltchinskii and Panchenko (2004), and show sparsity-type and cluster-variance-type generalization bounds for random classes.

findings.summary: Choosing projections from the data breaks a condition used in the proof. The classifier can fit every training example while having near-total true error despite a low certificate.
findings.claim: The claimed margin/generalization bounds apply to the advertised random kernel component classes with projections chosen from training data, using only the selected class cardinality and individual classifier complexities.
findings.location: Problem 2 and General problem, PDF pages 4–6 (printed 310–312); Theorem 2, equation (3.6), PDF page 7 (printed 313); claimed inheritance of (2.2)/(2.3), PDF page 18 (printed 324). Related Theorems 3–5, PDF pages 8–11.
findings.explanation: Data-adaptive projection selection need not preserve the incremental event-class property required by Theorem 1. A permitted fixed-Gaussian, two-projection class has four functions, fits every training point with margin 0.9, and has true error at least 0.99, while Theorem 2 certifies at most 0.26230008. The contradiction holds for every sample.
findings.evidence: For n = 10000, M = 1000000, let X be uniform on x_j = (2 sqrt(M) e_j,1), Y = +1. Project first onto the unit sum of unseen coordinate directions and second onto the last coordinate. With fixed Gaussian K(a,b) = exp(−(a−b)^2), the selected class is {±g_S,±1}, so G*(2n) = 4. The classifier (19/20)g_S − 1/20 has training margin 9/10 and negative score on every unseen point, giving error 1−|S|/M >= 0.99. At delta = 2/5 and t = ln(20), equation (3.6) gives U = 0.065500029536 and bound 0.262300080006; the coarse rational certificate is below 0.2877 < 0.99. When all support points have been observed, a unit normal annihilating all x_j defines a valid fallback, keeping selected cardinality <= 4 at every sample size. The old error level set cannot belong to the new margin class because every newly selected base function has equal values on an old and newly observed point. Conditional incremental Theorem 1 is not refuted.
findings.impact: Extending margin, sparsity and clustering bounds to data-selected kernel/component classes is an explicit central contribution. The claimed selected-class complexity ignores adaptive selection and can certify small error for a class with nearly unit true error. Larger finite domains and samples make the discrepancy unbounded relative to the stated rate, so a constant correction does not repair it. Requiring nested classes preserves conditional Theorem 1 and fixed-kernel SVM/stump cases but withdraws the expressly permitted arbitrary learned-projection application or requires a new complexity analysis of class selection.

papers.title: Analysis of Variance of Cross-Validation Estimators of the Generalization Error
papers.abstract: This paper brings together methods from two different disciplines: statistics and machine learning. We address the problem of estimating the variance of cross-validation (CV) estimators of the generalization error. In particular, we approach the problem of variance estimation of the CV estimators of generalization error as a problem in approximating the moments of a statistic. The approximation illustrates the role of training and test sets in the performance of the algorithm. It provides a unifying approach to evaluation of various methods used in obtaining training and test sets and it takes into account the variability due to different training and test sets. For the simple problem of predicting the sample mean and in the case of smooth loss functions, we show that the variance of the CV estimator of the generalization error is a function of the moments of the random variables Y=Card(Sj ∩ Sj') and Y*=Card(Sjc ∩ Sj'c), where Sj, Sj' are two training sets, and Sjc, Sj'c are the corresponding test sets. We prove that the distribution of Y and Y* is hypergeometric and we compare our estimator with the one proposed by Nadeau and Bengio (2003). We extend these results in the regression case and the case of absolute error loss, and indicate how the methods can be extended to the classification case. We illustrate the results through simulation.

findings.summary: The cross-validation variance formula omits dependence created when examples exchange training and test roles. For allowed smooth losses, this materially understates the variability of the evaluation.
findings.claim: The general smooth-loss moment-approximation estimator correctly estimates cross-validation variance through first order, accounting for train/test overlap, with an O(n1^-2) remainder.
findings.location: Proposition 3.3, Theorem 3.1 and k-fold specialization, PDF pages 8–11 (printed 1134–1137); Lemma B.4, PDF pages 34–35 (1160–1161); Appendix C equations (3)–(4), PDF page 37 (1163).
findings.explanation: The cross-split covariance calculation drops first-order dependence when an observation is tested in one split and trained on in another. For bounded skew data and a globally smooth convex loss, n times the true CV variance tends to 0.4 while the proposed formula tends to 0.210138344784. A Gaussian shifted-square loss gives an exact datasetwise cancellation that the proposed leading formula violates.
findings.evidence: With P(X=-1)=2/3, P(X=2)=1/3 and L(t,x)=sqrt(1+(t-x)^2)-1, all moments exist, fourth derivatives of L and L squared are bounded by 15 and 30, and true leading variance is Var(L(0,X)+dX)=2/5. The paper gives Var(L(0,X))+2d^2=(98-28sqrt(10))/45=0.210138344784, omitting 2d Cov(L(0,X),X)=0.189861655216. Independently, for Gaussian X and L_c=(t-x-c)^2, balanced complete k-fold CV_c=CV_0+c^2 for every dataset, so true variance is independent of c and equals 2/n+2[-k+k^4/(k-1)^3]/n^2. The printed general formula adds 8c^2/n. For c=1 its leading coefficient is five times the truth, and the discrepancy cannot be O(n^-2). Independent random CV likewise has an erroneous added 8c^2(J-1)/(Jn). Exact finite comparisons are illustrative, not reliance on an unspecified finite remainder.
findings.impact: General smooth-loss CV variance estimation is the central advertised contribution. The main covariance theorem and proposed estimator miss a term of the same order as the target variance, producing a nonvanishing relative error under ordinary admissible data/losses. Repair requires rederiving the main covariance formula and estimator or withdrawing substantial generality; it is not a second-order constant or isolated table correction. Hypergeometric overlap identities and leading symmetric squared-loss results remain unrefuted.

papers.title: Algorithmic Stability and Meta-Learning
papers.abstract: A mechnism of transfer learning is analysed, where samples drawn from different learning tasks of an environment are used to improve the learners performance on a new task. We give a general method to prove generalisation error bounds for such meta-algorithms. The method can be applied to the bias learning model of J. Baxter and to derive novel generalisation bounds for meta-algorithms searching spaces of uniformly stable algorithms. We also present an application to regularized least squares regression.

findings.summary: The transfer-risk bound drops residual uncertainty in the prediction targets. Strong regularization can produce a tiny certificate even though the true prediction loss remains large.
findings.claim: The CP-regression meta-algorithm has the explicit high-confidence transfer-risk upper bound (36), with task-sampling confidence penalty proportional to 1/lambda and ordinary estimation term 4/(m lambda).
findings.location: Equation (36), PDF page 24 (printed 990); squared-loss range and ordinary stability claim, PDF page 21 (987); repeated stability claim on PDF page 23 (989). The CP-regression application is advertised in the abstract and PDF page 5.
findings.explanation: The loss range omits the target residual and incorrectly vanishes at large regularization. With admissible positive feature mixing, nonzero inputs and an ordinary ridge primer, equation (36) certifies transfer loss below 0.002 when true risk is 0.49995; the claimed 90% certificate fails with probability 25%.
findings.evidence: H=R, X={1}; the environment equally mixes deterministic tasks with labels 0 and 1. Set m=n=2, mu=1/2, lambda=10000, delta=1/10, and use ordinary ridge primer lambda0=1 with valid kappa=1. Both training tasks have label zero with probability 1/4, giving learned inner product ab/2 and empirical meta-loss zero. True transfer risk is 200000000/400040001≈0.499950003750; printed equation (36) is [6+17sqrt(ln(10)/4)]/10000≈0.001889813060. Since ln(10)<4, the bound is strictly below23/10000<49/100<true risk. Failure is exactly1/4 across the four equiprobable cases. The loss range 1/lambda is false; a target-one residual remains near one as lambda grows. Related unclipped ridge stability2/(lambda m) is also false at lambda=.01, m=10000, with exact test-loss change11915/39601>.02, but the decisive risk witness does not rely on that secondary defect.
findings.impact: The sole fully worked algorithmic application is separately advertised and supplies a false quantitative transfer-risk certificate: its task-sampling uncertainty disappears under large regularization even though environmental label uncertainty persists. The false regularization dependence cannot be corrected by any universal constant factor. The application requires corrected loss-range/stability analysis and a changed displayed guarantee. The general meta-learning reduction and Theorems1,4–6 under valid assumptions, as well as CP empirical meta-stability, remain unrefuted; corrected fixed-parameter sample-size rates can survive.

papers.title: An MDP-Based Recommender System
papers.abstract: Typical recommender systems adopt a static view of the recommendation process and treat it as a prediction problem. We argue that it is more appropriate to view the problem of generating recommendations as a sequential optimization problem and, consequently, that Markov decision processes (MDPs) provide a more appropriate model for recommender systems. MDPs introduce two benefits: they take into account the long-term effects of each recommendation and the expected value of each recommendation. To succeed in practice, an MDP-based recommender system must employ a strong initial model, must be solvable quickly, and should not consume too much memory. In this paper, we describe our particular MDP model, its initialization using a predictive model, the solution and update algorithm, and its actual performance on a commercial site. We also describe the particular predictive model we used which outperforms previous models. Our system is one of a small number of commercially deployed recommender systems. As far as we know, it is the first to report experimental analysis conducted on a real commercial site. These results validate the commercial value of recommender systems, and in particular, of our MDP-based approach.

findings.summary: The purchase update reverses a conditional probability. Transition probabilities may fail to sum to one, and normalizing them can still reverse which recommendation is judged best.
findings.claim: The online update estimates recommendation-dependent purchase transition probabilities for the MDP; these learned probabilities support simulated policy evaluation and the interpretation of the commercially deployed MDP model.
findings.location: PDF page 21 (printed 1285), Section 5.3, purchase-count definitions and equations (29)–(33); initialization continues on PDF22 (1286), equations (34)–(36). Affected learned-model simulation and deployed-model descriptions: PDF23–25 (1287–1289), Section6.1/Table3.
findings.explanation: The update divides purchases when shown/not shown by all purchases of the item, estimating recommendation inclusion conditional on purchase rather than purchase conditional on inclusion. Valid complete logs produce transition-row mass2.8; even a charitable row normalization can reverse the optimal recommendation list.
findings.evidence: Four items, lists of3, pin6/25,pout2/25,no-purchase1/5. Show each omission list100times with24 purchases of every included item,8 of the omitted and20 no-purchases. Each item has cin72,cout8,total80, so printed estimates.9/.1 give row14/5 and no-purchase residual−9/5; exposure denominators300/100 correctly give6/25 and2/25. Repeat data to eliminate any fixed prior. With omission-list visits2700/100/100/100, printed in=(1/4,87/88,87/88,87/88),out=(3/4,1/88,1/88,1/88). Next-item values(2,1,1,1) give true value22/25 when omitting1 versus26/25 when including1; normalizing printed purchase rows gives131/109 versus219/197 and chooses the worse omission. Multiplying normalized rows by4/5 to preserve the true no-purchase mass leaves the wrong choice.
findings.impact: The specified central learning procedure can fail to define a stochastic MDP and can learn action values that choose a strictly worse recommendation under its own response assumptions. Normalization alone cannot repair it: exposure counts, fitted rows and policy values must change, and the learned-model validation using those updates must be reassessed. The paper explicitly ties the simulator and deployed model to nearly a year of these updates. This refutes the learned-MDP specification and its validation as written, while preserving the general MDP idea and independent predictive-model contribution; it does not prove any unknown historical code or reported real commercial gain false.

papers.title: Matrix Exponentiated Gradient Updates for On-line Learning and Bregman Projection
papers.abstract: We address the problem of learning a symmetric positive definite matrix. The central issue is to design parameter updates that preserve positive definiteness. Our updates are motivated with the von Neumann divergence. Rather than treating the most general case, we focus on two key applications that exemplify our methods: on-line learning with a simple square loss, and finding a symmetric positive definite matrix subject to linear constraints. The updates generalize the exponentiated gradient (EG) update and AdaBoost, respectively: the parameter is now a symmetric positive definite matrix of trace one instead of a probability vector (which in this context is a diagonal positive definite matrix with trace one). The generalized updates use matrix logarithms and exponentials to preserve positive definiteness. Most importantly, we show how the derivation and the analyses of the original EG update and AdaBoost generalize to the non-diagonal case. We apply the resulting matrix exponentiated gradient (MEG) update and DefiniteBoost to the problem of learning a kernel matrix from distance measurements.

findings.summary: One-way multiplier updates can stop at a feasible matrix that is not optimal. The proposed projection solver can miss a better feasible solution to its stated objective.
findings.claim: DeﬁniteBoost/exact sequential projections solve the minimum von-Neumann-divergence projection problem (4.1), with global convergence to its optimum.
findings.location: PDF10 (printed1004),Section4.1/Eq4.1;PDF11 (1005),Figure1/Section4.2/Eqs4.3–4.5;PDF12 (1006),Section4.3/Eq4.6/Algorithm2; feasibility-only convergence argument PDF13–14.
findings.explanation: Positive-only multiplier updates can stop feasible but nonoptimal. Exact uniform five-dimensional diagonal example terminates after two exact projections while averaging two diagonal entries gives a strictly better feasible matrix.
findings.evidence: W1=I/5,CA=diag(1,1,1,-1,-1),CB=diag(1,1,-1,1,-1),bounds±1. Violationsinitial(1/5,1/5). Astep alpha=.5log(3/2) givesp=(1/6,1/6,1/6,1/4,1/4),violations(0,1/6). Bstep alpha=.5log(7/5) givesp=(1/7,1/7,1/5,3/14,3/10),violations(-1/35,0);algorithmstops. Averagingcoordinates3/4to29/140 givesstrictlypositivefeasiblematrixwithviolations(-1/70,-1/70) andstrictlysmaller sum p log(5p). Objectives.0402887944307352 vs.0400424401767718. Returnedprimal-dualgapexactlog(3/2)/70. Samefailureforany0<epsilon<1/6andmirroredinitialtie; individualstepsareexactBregmanprojections. Independent optimum.0349171448546120.
findings.impact: A principal advertised contribution is a minimum-divergence matrix projection solver preserving the prior subject to constraints. The supplied algorithm terminates at a demonstrably nonoptimal feasible matrix even with arbitrarily small feasibility tolerance. It needs multiplier-decrease/correction mechanisms, optimality stopping and changed convergence analysis; a sign/constant/line-search repair cannot suffice. Recasting it as feasibility abandons the explicit central objective and optimum-convergence guarantee. Separate MEG regret and symmetric-bound feasibility result survive; no historical classification-score failure is alleged.

papers.title: Expectation Correction for Smoothed Inference in Switching Linear Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract: We introduce a method for approximate smoothed inference in a class of switching linear dynamical systems, based on a novel form of Gaussian Sum smoother. This class includes the switching Kalman 'Filter' and the more general case of switch transitions dependent on the continuous latent state. The method improves on the standard Kim smoothing approach by dispensing with one of the key approximations, thus making fuller use of the available future information. Whilst the central assumption required is projection to a mixture of Gaussians, we show that an additional conditional independence assumption results in a simpler but accurate alternative. Our method consists of a single Forward and Backward Pass and is reminiscent of the standard smoothing 'correction' recursions in the simpler linear dynamical system. The method is numerically stable and compares favourably against alternative approximations, both in cases where a single mixture component provides a good posterior approximation, and where a multimodal approximation is required.

findings.summary: The hidden-state update ignores switching probabilities that depend on the state. The central inference construction uses an independence assumption inconsistent with the model it is intended to analyze.
findings.claim: The advertised augmented SLDS inference extension propagates the augmented model using Gaussian components before projection, with Gaussian-mixture collapse and the stated optional backward independence as its central approximations.
findings.location: PDF page 4 (journal 2518), Equation (5); page 5 Algorithm 1; page 8 (2522), Equation (11), following paragraph and footnote 8. Scope: abstract page 1, augmented model page 2, ADF/Figure 2 description pages 3–4, relaxed EC page 11.
findings.explanation: The continuous conditioning omits the state-dependent switch likelihood p(s_next|h,s), falsely treating the current hidden state as independent of the next switch. Scalar gate averaging in Algorithm 1 does not restore gate-weighted continuous moments; reverse conditioning has the same omission.
findings.evidence: Stable scalar dynamics A=.9 with process variance .01, initial variance1, smooth probit gate Phi(10h), switch-only emissions of bias +/-1 and variance1/16, observations (0,1,-1/50): exact final positive-switch posterior .89403818597357 versus printed .34524653939368, selecting opposite MAP states, with no component reduction. True time2 conditional hidden mean .71453233034389 versus zero. Exact independent path integration agrees below1e-12. Nonzero B=.001/.01 controls retain posterior error above.53.
findings.impact: The central claimed augmented-model ADF/projection-only extension uses a conditional-independence identity contradicting its own state-dependent switch model. It discards information before Gaussian projection and fails without truncation or the optional backward approximation. Repair requires gate-weighted non-Gaussian forward moments and reverse kernels, hence rederivation/additional approximation or withdrawal of that scope, not a local constant or index correction. Ordinary SLDS results and historical experimental scores are not alleged false.

papers.title: A Simulation-Based Algorithm for Ergodic Control of Markov Chains Conditioned on Rare Events
papers.abstract: We study the problem of long-run average cost control of Markov chains conditioned on a rare event. In a related recent work, a simulation based algorithm for estimating performance measures associated with a Markov chain conditioned on a rare event has been developed. We extend ideas from this work and develop an adaptive algorithm for obtaining, online, optimal control policies conditioned on a rare event. Our algorithm uses three timescales or step-size schedules. On the slowest timescale, a gradient search algorithm for policy updates that is based on one-simulation simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) type estimates is used. Deterministic perturbation sequences obtained from appropriate normalized Hadamard matrices are used here. The fast timescale recursions compute the conditional transition probabilities of an associated chain by obtaining solutions to the multiplicative Poisson equation (for a given policy estimate). Further, the risk parameter associated with the value function for a given policy estimate is updated on a timescale that lies in between the two scales above. We briefly sketch the convergence analysis of our algorithm and present a numerical application in the setting of routing multiple flows in communication networks.

findings.summary: The policy critic uses immediate cost where conditional long-run cost is required. The algorithm can stop changing an interior policy that is provably suboptimal.
findings.claim: The proposed adaptive control algorithm follows the gradient of the long-run average cost conditioned on the rare event and converges to stationary/local minimizing policies.
findings.location: PDF pages 9–10 (printed 1945–1946), Section 3.1: Y_i(0) = 0 and equations (7)–(8); PDF page 11 (1947), synchronous equations (11)–(12); PDF page 13 (1949), claimed cost tracking and projected-gradient ODE (14); PDF page 14 (1950), convergence to Kuhn–Tucker points/local minima. Contribution scope: abstract/introduction, problem definition and PDF page 23 conclusion.
findings.explanation: The state-specific cost critic averages a one-step original-chain cost instead of the conditioned stationary average. A zero immediate cost at a state freezes that state’s policy even when it strictly changes future conditioned cost. A strictly positive three-state example freezes the prescribed interior policy at theta = 1/2 with true gradient −1/16 and optimality gap 1/28.
findings.evidence: Three states, two actions: state 1 has rows A = (3/5, 1/5, 1/5), B = (1/5, 3/5, 1/5); both actions at states 2 and 3 have row (2/5, 2/5, 1/5). Let g = 1_{state 3}, alpha = 1/2, h = 1_{current state 2}. All action transitions are positive and every original stationary g mean is 1/5. For probability theta of action A at state 1, tilted PF eigenvector is (1, 1, z), eigenvalue (4+z)/5 and optimal z = 4. The conditioned kernel has first row (1/8 + theta/4, 3/8 − theta/4, 1/2), other rows (1/4, 1/4, 1/2). Its stationary law is (2/(9−2theta), 1/2−2/(9−2theta), 1/2); hence J = 1/2−2/(9−2theta) and J prime = −4/(9−2theta)^2. At theta = 1/2, J = 1/4 and J prime = −1/16, but h(1,a,j) = 0 and Y_1(0) = 0 force Y_1 = 0 and theta_1 = 1/2 forever. The optimum theta = 1 has J = 3/14, leaving gap 1/28. For delta <= 1/4 the perturbed output still has gap >= 2/105. The critic targets are (0, 1, 0), not J. The Step 0 dimension typo is charitably corrected; the witness works with every valid perturbation.
findings.impact: Conditioned policy learning is the main new contribution beyond prior fixed-policy conditional-performance estimation. The actual algorithm can freeze a strictly improving interior coordinate even with perfect conditioned-transition estimates, invalidating its gradient and stationary-policy convergence claims. Fixing a likelihood ratio, step-size constant, perturbation sign or local/global qualifier does not repair the state-specific immediate-cost critic. A global-average or appropriate cost-to-go estimator and a new policy-gradient/convergence analysis are required. Fixed-policy conditioning results and the possibility of the reported routing behavior remain unrefuted; no historical implementation or corrected numerical ranking is asserted.

papers.title: A Robust Procedure For Gaussian Graphical Model Search From Microarray Data With p Larger Than n
papers.abstract: Learning of large-scale networks of interactions from microarray data is an important and challenging problem in bioinformatics. A widely used approach is to assume that the available data constitute a random sample from a multivariate distribution belonging to a Gaussian graphical model. As a consequence, the prime objects of inference are full-order partial correlations which are partial correlations between two variables given the remaining ones. In the context of microarray data the number of variables exceed the sample size and this precludes the application of traditional structure learning procedures because a sampling version of full-order partial correlations does not exist. In this paper we consider limited-order partial correlations, these are partial correlations computed on marginal distributions of manageable size, and provide a set of rules that allow one to assess the usefulness of these quantities to derive the independence structure of the underlying Gaussian graphical model. Furthermore, we introduce a novel structure learning procedure based on a quantity, obtained from limited-order partial correlations, that we call the non-rejection rate. The applicability and usefulness of the procedure are demonstrated by both simulated and real data.

findings.summary: Full-rank clique statistics do not ensure an estimable fit for the stated nondecomposable model. The stopping rule can approve a case with unbounded likelihood.
findings.claim: A selected Gaussian graphical model and its submodels can be fitted by standard techniques whenever its largest clique is smaller than the sample size. This criterion drives threshold selection for arbitrary undirected graphs.
findings.location: PDF page 6 (journal 2626), final paragraph; Section 5.2, PDF pages 13–14 (2633–2634), qp-clique rule; PDF page 17 (2637), threshold selection. Original qp 0.1-1 R/qp.R lines 222–270.
findings.explanation: Full-rank clique statistics are not sufficient for nondecomposable models. An allowed default-level n = 29, p = 30, q = 0 sample selects join(K26,C4), with maximum clique 28 < 29 and an unbounded Gaussian likelihood.
findings.evidence: Core vectors at angles 0, 45, 90, 135 degrees, with 26 nuisance rows .99 h + sqrt(.0199)e_j and h at 67.5 degrees. The weakest retained-edge correlation is .3788565980414, with exact two-sided t27 p = .04269078032891 < .05; deleted core pairs have p = 1. All 500 q = 0 tests give NRR 0 or 1, so beta*=.949 selects the graph. Supported K0 has positive eigenvalues 2sqrt2, annihilates U, and makes logdet(I+tK0) diverge while tr(SK0)=0. Strict positivity/decisions persist on an open sample neighborhood. Historical SDP is numerical corroboration only.
findings.impact: The actual stopping rule can approve a model for which ordinary likelihood fitting has no solution, invalidating the advertised reduction to a fittable Gaussian-model search space. Repair requires a global completion/likelihood-existence condition or a graph-class restriction and corresponding threshold/model-selection changes. Correct q-partial graph theory and historical empirical scores are not claimed false.

papers.title: Optimising Kernel Parameters and Regularisation Coefficients for Non-linear Discriminant Analysis
papers.abstract: In this paper we consider a novel Bayesian interpretation of Fisher's discriminant analysis. We relate Rayleigh's coefficient to a noise model that minimises a cost based on the most probable class centres and that abandons the 'regression to the labels' assumption used by other algorithms. Optimisation of the noise model yields a direction of discrimination equivalent to Fisher's discriminant, and with the incorporation of a prior we can apply Bayes' rule to infer the posterior distribution of the direction of discrimination. Nonetheless, we argue that an additional constraining distribution has to be included if sensible results are to be obtained. Going further, with the use of a Gaussian process prior we show the equivalence of our model to a regularised kernel Fisher's discriminant. A key advantage of our approach is the facility to determine kernel parameters and the regularisation coefficient through the optimisation of the marginal log-likelihood of the data. An added bonus of the new formulation is that it enables us to link the regularisation coefficient with the generalisation error.

findings.summary: The precision update can reduce the stated learning objective. Correcting it still permits the kernel to shrink toward a degenerate boundary, undermining the proposed principled parameter-learning procedure.
findings.claim: The proposed Bayesian discriminant automatically determines kernel parameters and regularization by a convergent EM maximization of marginal likelihood.
findings.location: PDF pages 18–20 (printed 472–474), Section 7, Equations (29)–(32) and Algorithm 1; separating constraint on PDF pages 12–13, Equations (20)–(23); freely scaled RBF+nugget family on PDF page 34, Equation (47). Centrality: abstract PDF page 1 and conclusion PDF pages 27–28.
findings.explanation: The zero-mean E-step and constrained-predictor precision statistic are inconsistent, so a complete exact allowed M-step plus the stated precision update decreases the declared evidence. Correcting that statistic alone leaves an objective that strictly rewards shrinking all kernel amplitudes toward a degenerate boundary because the separating constraint is absent from the learning evidence.
findings.evidence: With inputs (0,0,1,1), class labels (0,0,1,1), beta=1 and d=2, RBF+nugget parameters (1,2 log2,1) admit an exact kernel M-step (5/4,2 log(5/2),1/2) with Knew=Sigma_old. The constrained training variance is 7/6 per point, so Eq.32 sets beta=9/17 and H decreases from -1.19314718056 to -1.45352862351. The source cross-kernel convention also decreases H, including all parameter clamps. For K=aK0, H=(N-1)log(beta)/2-beta/2-logdet(I+beta aK0L)/2 has strictly negative derivative in log a for L nonzero. A trace correction restores EM only for this collapsing objective; conditioning on nonzero d changes the evidence, E-posterior and both M-step statistics.
findings.impact: Automatic principled marginal-likelihood determination of kernel parameters and regularization is a main advertised contribution and drives the experimental parameter selection. Its stated EM update can lower its objective, while actually maximizing that objective has no nondegenerate interior scale optimum. Repair requires a different constrained evidence/posterior or added model restrictions, not merely the local precision-statistic correction. The fixed-parameter Bayesian/KFD equivalence and reported AUC values are not claimed disproved.

papers.title: Statistical Comparisons of Classifiers over Multiple Data Sets
papers.abstract: While methods for comparing two learning algorithms on a single data set have been scrutinized for quite some time already, the issue of statistical tests for comparisons of more algorithms on multiple data sets, which is even more essential to typical machine learning studies, has been all but ignored. This article reviews the current practice and then theoretically and empirically examines several suitable tests. Based on that, we recommend a set of simple, yet safe and robust non-parametric tests for statistical comparisons of classifiers: the Wilcoxon signed ranks test for comparison of two classifiers and the Friedman test with the corresponding post-hoc tests for comparison of more classifiers over multiple data sets. Results of the latter can also be neatly presented with the newly introduced CD (critical difference) diagrams.

findings.summary: Equal marginal performance does not ensure the dependence between ranks required by the test. An allowed example rejects a true null more often than advertised, undermining error calibration.
findings.claim: Safe nominal-level comparison of equivalent classifiers over independent data sets, using Friedman followed by Nemenyi without a within-data-set exchangeability/rank-covariance condition.
findings.location: PDF pages 2 and 5 (setup/independence), page 10 (sphericity discussion), pages 11–12, Section 3.2.2 and Table 5(a) (Friedman/Iman–Davenport and Nemenyi calibration), page 27 (general applicability recommendation).
findings.explanation: Equal marginal performance distributions and expected ranks do not imply the permutation rank covariance required by the printed null laws. An admissible six-classifier, 20-independent-data-set example gives exact false rejection 15115/131072 = 0.11531829833984375; a strictly positive continuous-density variant has rigorous lower bound 0.1125824351222488.
findings.evidence: For ranks (1,2,3,4,5,6) or reverse equiprobably, chi_F² = 5(2B−20)²/20. Both omnibus variants and Nemenyi reject iff B≤6 or B≥14, giving the exact binomial tail. The limit law is 5Z² rather than chi-square_5. Marginal score laws are all exactly Uniform(0,1). Circular triangular noise and a 0.001 independent-uniform mixture give continuous density bounded below while preserving a >0.11 rejection lower bound. This is outside the classical stronger joint-exchangeability null, which the paper does not state.
findings.impact: The safe applicability and calibration of the multiple-classifier procedure is a principal contribution. Correcting it requires narrowing the substantive null to joint exchangeability or changing the inferential procedure; ordinary table corrections or more data do not preserve the promised classifier-equivalence calibration. Classical Friedman/Nemenyi under joint exchangeability and historical empirical outputs are not alleged false.

papers.title: Learning Sparse Representations by Non-Negative Matrix Factorization and Sequential Cone Programming
papers.abstract: We exploit the biconvex nature of the Euclidean non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) optimization problem to derive optimization schemes based on sequential quadratic and second order cone programming. We show that for ordinary NMF, our approach performs as well as existing state-of-the-art algorithms, while for sparsity-constrained NMF, as recently proposed by P. O. Hoyer in JMLR 5 (2004), it outperforms previous methods. In addition, we show how to extend NMF learning within the same optimization framework in order to make use of class membership information in supervised learning problems.

findings.summary: The sparsity constraint is not convex and the prescribed step can become stuck at an infeasible factor. The fallback procedure lacks its advertised guaranteed convergence.
findings.claim: SMA preserves minimum sparsity and supplies a guaranteed-convergent alternative for sparse NMF from the arbitrary boundary initialization explicitly allowed in the text.
findings.location: PDF page 13 (printed 1397), Section 5.3.1, Equation (38c), its convexity/feasibility assertion and arbitrary-boundary initialization; PDF page 14 (1398), Equations (40b)–(41); PDF page 15 (1399), Algorithm 5.2 and Proposition 10. The direct counterexample concerns the general prose-authorized boundary start, not the particular suggested projection initializer.
findings.explanation: Normalized Hoyer sparsity is not convex. The rowwise affine max-min step can set a feasible factor row exactly uniform, after which the distance-to-cone step has radius zero and fixes an infeasible factor. A two-iteration exact counterexample satisfies the stated rank, interval and essentiality assumptions.
findings.evidence: W=I2, V=[[100,200,150],[.3,.3,.3]], H0=[[2/3,1/3,1],[.1,.3,.2]], smin_h=sp(1,2,3)≈.1755115284, smax_h=1. First full H iterate has sparsities .2235906353 and .9885130449. The next unique Equation 38 optimum has t≈.3385297484 and row2 exactly (.3,.3,.3), with affine slack>.6288 but actual sparsity 0. Equation 40 fixes that row because its cone distance is zero. The uniform row has zero sparsity gradient, permitting later optimal t=0/current-factor selections that keep it infeasible. With smin_w=sp(1,10^-6), all exact nonnegative factorizations satisfying W sparsity force a loading row with sparsity<.001184, proving essentiality. The witness uses the prose-authorized arbitrary boundary initialization; it does not establish a failure of the specific suggested projection initializer.
findings.impact: The paper specifically presents SMA as its guaranteed-convergent sparse NMF fallback when TPC oscillates. Under the arbitrary boundary initialization expressly permitted in Section 5.3.1, exactly solved SMA subproblems violate the defining minimum-sparsity constraint and admit permanently infeasible H-block continuations. The general feasibility guarantee must therefore be withdrawn or the method changed; replacing normalized sparsity by a scale-dependent convex margin changes the stated max-min objective. This is not an ordinary constant or notation correction. The particular projection initializer in Algorithm 5.2 remains unrefuted, and the absence of a replacement proof for a restricted version is not an additional finding. TPC, ordinary NNLS and historical empirical comparisons are not claimed invalid.

papers.title: Learning Coordinate Covariances via Gradients
papers.abstract: We introduce an algorithm that learns gradients from samples in the supervised learning framework. An error analysis is given for the convergence of the gradient estimated by the algorithm to the true gradient. The utility of the algorithm for the problem of variable selection as well as determining variable covariance is illustrated on simulated data as well as two gene expression data sets. For square loss we provide a very efficient implementation with respect to both memory and time.

findings.summary: The gradient-learning proof uses a spectral identity under the wrong weighting of the data. An allowed example violates the claimed convergence rate, so it does not hold as stated.
findings.claim: The population gradient error in L2(rhoX) is bounded by C s/lambda plus a fixed sqrt(lambda) term under gradient-in-RKHS and Hölder/boundary conditions, supporting Section4’s advertised convergence/error analysis and intended sample rate.

A C3 disjoint-bump kernel withp(x)=2x, bounded deterministic responses and gradient inHK violates Proposition15 by a certified factor>4; the same fixed example defeats any constant in the intended decaying sample rate.

Its foundational regularization proposition is false under its own assumptions, and the intended rate cannot be restored by correcting constants or exponent typography. An added positive density lower bound, changed metric or different-rate theorem is required. The solver and descriptive experiments do not establish the missing guarantee; their historical outcomes are not claimed false.

papers.title: Policy Gradient in Continuous Time
papers.abstract: Policy search is a method for approximately solving an optimal control problem by performing a parametric optimization search in a given class of parameterized policies. In order to process a local optimization technique, such as a gradient method, we wish to evaluate the sensitivity of the performance measure with respect to the policy parameters, the so-called policy gradient. This paper is concerned with the estimation of the policy gradient for continuous-time, deterministic state dynamics, in a reinforcement learning framework, that is, when the decision maker does not have a model of the state dynamics. We show that usual likelihood ratio methods used in discrete-time, fail to proceed the gradient because they are subject to variance explosion when the discretization time-step decreases to 0. We describe an alternative approach based on the approximation of the pathwise derivative, which leads to a policy gradient estimate that converges almost surely to the true gradient when the timestep tends to 0. The underlying idea starts with the derivation of an explicit representation of the policy gradient using pathwise derivation. This derivation makes use of the knowledge of the state dynamics. Then, in order to estimate the gradient from the observable data only, we use a stochastic policy to discretize the continuous deterministic system into a stochastic discrete process, which enables to replace the unknown coefficients by quantities that solely depend on known data. We prove the almost sure convergence of this estimate to the true policy gradient when the discretization time-step goes to zero. The method is illustrated on two target problems, in discrete and continuous control spaces.

findings.summary: The continuous-action implementation has persistent exploration noise and a singular regression problem. The advertised direct control method needs additional conditions and a revised construction to support its implementation.
findings.claim: The model-free single-trajectory gradient estimator and its almost-sure convergence extend directly to continuous controls using Gaussian perturbations with v(Delta) tending to zero.
findings.location: PDF page 12 (printed 782), Section 3.5; PDF page 11 (printed 781), Eq. (24); PDF pages 8–10, exact-action regression; PDF page 14 (printed 784), v(Delta)=Delta experimental schedule.
findings.explanation: The experimental noise schedule leaves a nonvanishing score-noise term, while the specified continuous-action Jacobian regression is almost surely singular.

(24) gives Z_N=sqrt(Delta)sum G+sqrt(Delta)sum G*tanh(sqrt(Delta)G), where the first term is N(0,1) and the second converges to1 in L2. Hence Z_N tends in law to N(1,1), not in probability to1, even though the state converges. Exact-action Gaussian tables each contain one midpoint and have covariance0, so changing the schedule alone does not restore the literal model-free procedure.
findings.impact: One of the advertised continuous-control contributions and its claimed direct model-free implementation require a different exploration condition and a new regression construction/analysis. This is more than a local formula correction. Finite-action results and historical achieved rewards are not alleged false.

papers.title: Learning the Structure of Linear Latent Variable Models
papers.abstract: We describe anytime search procedures that (1) find disjoint subsets of recorded variables for which the members of each subset are d-separated by a single common unrecorded cause, if such exists; (2) return information about the causal relations among the latent factors so identified. We prove the procedure is point-wise consistent assuming (a) the causal relations can be represented by a directed acyclic graph (DAG) satisfying the Markov Assumption and the Faithfulness Assumption; (b) unrecorded variables are not caused by recorded variables; and (c) dependencies are linear. We compare the procedure with standard approaches over a variety of simulated structures and sample sizes, and illustrate its practical value with brief studies of social science data sets. Finally, we consider generalizations for non-linear systems.

findings.summary: The conditional-independence assumptions do not ensure structural equalities used by the algorithm. It can report a single hidden cause when no true cause has the required role.
findings.claim: The central pointwise recovery of genuine latent causal clusters under A1–A4, specifically the injective map from reported latent nodes to actual generating latent nodes with the separator property in Theorem 15.
findings.location: A4 and Definition 1: PDF 7 (journal 197); Lemma 9: PDF 10 (200); FINDPATTERN: PDF 12, Table 1; Theorem 15(1): PDF 16 (206) and PDF 52 (242); full BUILDPURECLUSTERS: PDF 37, Table 6; Theorem 21/proof: PDF 45 (235); pointwise claim: PDF 21 (211), abstract PDF 1 and conclusion PDF 36.
findings.explanation: CI faithfulness does not make population tetrad equalities structurally entailed. Two independent Gaussian roots, each loading identically on four noisy indicators, satisfy A1–A4 yet cause full BPC to return a four-child single-latent cluster for which neither true root is a separator.
findings.evidence: L1,L2 iid N(0,1), Xi=L1+L2+epsilon_i with independent error variances 1,2,3,4. Joint leading principal minors are 1,1,1,2,6,24. Observed off-diagonal covariance is 2, all tetrad products are 4, and every observed first-order partial covariance is positive. Neither root separates indicators (conditional covariance 1). Full Table 6 retains the unique four-indicator cluster; Theorem 15 has no valid actual-node map. The same observed law has a genuine one-factor representation, making the missing premise an identifiability issue. Later linear rank-faithfulness and generic-parameter guarantees are explicitly preserved as narrower possible repairs.
findings.impact: The paper expressly advertises proved actual-latent causal recovery under ordinary CI-faithfulness, and its population output violates that guarantee on a model satisfying every stated assumption. Observational indistinguishability prevents more data or adjusted thresholds from repairing it. Requiring rank/tetrad faithfulness substantively narrows the core identification premise and withdraws the advertised pointwise A1–A4 scope; generic versions and reported empirical results remain unrefuted.

papers.title: A Generalized Maximum Entropy Approach to Bregman Co-clustering and Matrix Approximation
papers.abstract: Co-clustering, or simultaneous clustering of rows and columns of a two-dimensional data matrix, is rapidly becoming a powerful data analysis technique. Co-clustering has enjoyed wide success in varied application domains such as text clustering, gene-microarray analysis, natural language processing and image, speech and video analysis. In this paper, we introduce a partitional co-clustering formulation that is driven by the search for a good matrix approximation---every co-clustering is associated with an approximation of the original data matrix and the quality of co-clustering is determined by the approximation error. We allow the approximation error to be measured using a large class of loss functions called Bregman divergences that include squared Euclidean distance and KL-divergence as special cases. In addition, we permit multiple structurally different co-clustering schemes that preserve various linear statistics of the original data matrix. To accomplish the above tasks, we introduce a new minimum Bregman information (MBI) principle that simultaneously generalizes the maximum entropy and standard least squares principles, and leads to a matrix approximation that is optimal among all generalized additive models in a certain natural parameter space. Analysis based on this principle yields an elegant meta algorithm, special cases of which include most previously known alternate minimization based clustering algorithms such as kmeans and co-clustering algorithms such as information theoretic (Dhillon et al., 2003b) and minimum sum-squared residue co-clustering (Cho et al., 2004). To demonstrate the generality and flexibility of our co-clustering framework, we provide examples and empirical evidence on a variety of problem domains and also describe novel co-clustering applications such as missing value prediction and compression of categorical data matrices.

findings.summary: Updates derived for independent weights are applied to arbitrary weights. In the missing-data setting, they can violate constraints and lose the promised decrease in the objective.
findings.claim: For arbitrary entry weights, the stated squared-error and I-divergence closed-form reconstructions solve the MBI problem, preserve its selected statistics, and instantiate the monotone efficient co-clustering algorithm, including missing-value prediction.
findings.location: PDF 6 and 9, arbitrary weighted extension; PDF 21 equations (17)–(18); PDF 22–23 Tables 1–2; PDF 31–32 closed-form specialization and Theorem 6 application; PDF 41–42 MovieLens/missing-data application; Appendix E, PDF 54 and 58–61, Tables 9–14.
findings.explanation: Conditional-mean formulas valid for product/uniform measures are applied to arbitrary nonproduct weights. Their outputs can violate the defining constraints and lose the exact-MBI descent guarantee.
